column2: How much are 13 and 15 added up?
column4: “How much are 13 and 15 added up?” is ungrammatical; a natural version is “What do 13 and 15 add up to?”

column2: January 18, 1868
column4: This is a date fragment, not a sentence.

column2: September 9th, 6 o'clock a.m.
column4: This is a date-and-time phrase, not a sentence.

column2: one person
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column1: 一个人住，洗衣服、做饭什么的都要自己做。
column2: When you live alone, laundry, cooking, and so on all need to be done yourself.
column4: “Laundry, cooking, and so on all need to be done yourself” is awkward and ungrammatical; the chores need to be done by you.

column1: 一个人帮不了许多个，但许多人能帮助一个。
column2: One can't help many, but many can help one.
column4: “帮不了许多个” is awkward without a noun; “一个人帮不了很多人” is natural.

column1: 一些司机笑的笑，喊的喊。
column2: Some of the drivers were laughing and yelling.
column4: “一些司机笑的笑，喊的喊” is not a natural way to describe what the drivers were doing.

column2: A group of youths play ball.
column4: 打球 describes people playing ball now; “play ball” suggests a habitual activity.

column2: Down fell the house a week later.
column4: “Down fell the house” is an unnatural, archaic inversion in ordinary English.

column1: 一想到家里有只猫在，我就全身不自在。
column2: I don't feel like myself, knowing there's a cat in my house.
column4: “全身不自在” means feeling uncomfortable or uneasy, not “not feeling like myself.”

column1: 一斤四元五毛，便宜得不得了！
column2: 4.5 yuan for one pound, now isn't that cheap!
column4: 一斤 is 500 grams, not one pound.

column1: 一方面要工作，另一方面要休息。
column2: On one hand work, on the other rest.
column4: “On one hand work, on the other rest” is not a natural English sentence.

column2: A straw and a roll of paper.
column4: Both sides are noun phrases, not sentences.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: one and a half bottles of wine
column4: 白酒 means Chinese spirits or liquor, not wine.

column2: A crowd waited to see him.
column4: 等着 describes waiting, while “waited” places it in the past.

column2: placeholder
column4: The English is only a placeholder, not a translatable sentence.

column2: A bag of rice and a box of fruit.
column4: Both sides are noun phrases, not sentences.

column1: 七月份，这条河不适合游泳。
column2: This river is dangerous to swim in, in July.
column4: 不适合游泳 means the river is not suitable for swimming, not necessarily dangerous.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: three iPhones
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: Three students.
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: 7 o'clock a.m.
column4: This is a time fragment, not a sentence.

column1: 上大学的时候，你得到的比付出的还多。
column2: You gain more than you spend when you go to college.
column4: “付出的” means what you put in or give, not specifically what you spend.

column2: God created the heaven and the earth.
column4: “the heaven and the earth”不自然；通常说“the heavens and the earth”。

column1: 上海人普通话说得怎么样？
column2: What does Shanghai people's Mandarin sound like?
column4: The Chinese asks how well Shanghai people speak Mandarin; the English asks what their Mandarin sounds like.

column2: Winter in Shanghai is a bit too cold.
column4: 有一点冷 means “a little cold,” not “a bit too cold.”

column2: Shanghai's weather
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: Office workers are busy daily.
column4: “Busy daily” is unnatural; say “busy every day.”

column1: 上课中不要跟别人讲话。
column2: Don't talk to others during the class.
column4: 上课中 is unnatural here; 上课时 would be the natural phrasing.

column1: 下个月我要到美国出差。
column2: Next month I need to go to the USA on a business trip.
column4: “我要” here means “I’m going to” or “I plan to,” not necessarily “I need to.”
This is a time phrase, not a sentence.

column2: 4 o'clock p.m.
column4: This is a time fragment, not a sentence.

column2: See you Monday at school.
column4: “下周一” means next Monday, but the English only says Monday.

column1: 下班以后你想跟我们一起去打球吗?
column2: After we get off work, would you like to go play ball with us?
column4: The Chinese means “After you get off work,” not “After we get off work.”

column1: 下礼拜我要去拜访她一下。
column2: I'm going to visit him next week.
column4: The Chinese says “她” (her), but the English says “him”.

column2: He wears a raincoat in rain.
column4: “下雨他穿雨衣” is awkward; a native speaker would usually say “下雨时他穿雨衣”.

column1: 下面写上我们班同学的名字。
column2: Underneath we wrote the names of the students in our class.
column4: The Chinese is an instruction to write the names underneath; the English says that we already wrote them.

column1: 不久派对完结，大家也都回家去了。
column2: By and by the party ended and everyone went home.
column4: “不久派对完结” is not a natural way to say “the party ended soon”; say “派对结束不久”.

column2: I won't do it again.
column4: The Chinese says there won't be a next time, without specifying who will do what; the English says the speaker won't do it again.

column2: I don't care.
column4: “不关我的事” means “It’s none of my business,” not “I don’t care.”

column2: There are many good reasons not to do it.
column4: The Chinese says there are many reasons it cannot be done; the English adds “good” and frames them as reasons not to do it.

column2: No more sitting.
column4: 不坐了 means “I won’t sit” or “I’m not sitting anymore,” while “No more sitting” sounds like a prohibition.

column1: 不好意思，我刚才出去了。
column2: I'm sorry, I just now stepped out.
column4: “I just now stepped out” is unnatural English; say “I just stepped out.”

column1: 不怕被人利用，就怕你没用。
column2: Don't fear being put upon. Fear instead being unable to help.
column4: “没用” means useless, not specifically unable to help.

column1: 不想做是原因；不能做仅仅是接口。
column2: Not wanting to is the reason; not being able to is just an excuse.
column4: “接口” means “interface”; “借口” (“excuse”) is needed here.

column1: 不愉快的感觉永远不好。
column2: An unpleasant feeling is always bad.
column4: “不愉快的感觉永远不好” is not a natural way to express that an unpleasant feeling is always bad.

column2: Ignore it.
column4: “不放在眼里” is a context-dependent phrase rather than a complete sentence.

column2: We don't know exactly.
column4: “不是特别清楚” means “(it’s) not particularly clear,” not “We don’t know exactly.”

column1: 不注意安全，后果很重大。
column2: Ignore safety and the consequences are serious.
column4: “后果很重大” is an unnatural collocation here; say “后果很严重.”

column2: Don't you know what that is?
column4: “那间” means “that room”; “哪间” is needed for “which room.”

column1: 不管他的理由是什么，总之，我不会再相信他了。
column4: The English translation is missing.

column1: 不管你怎么做，结果都一样。
column2: Regardless what you may do, the outcome will still be the same.
column4: “Regardless” needs “of” here: “Regardless of what you may do…”

column1: 不管哪几本，就选择三本书吧。
column2: It doesn't matter which, just pick three books.
column4: “不管哪几本” is awkward here; “不管是哪几本” would be more natural.

column2: However hard, persist.
column4: “However hard, persist” is awkward; a natural version is “No matter how hard it is, keep going.”

column2: Don't rely only on parents.
column4: 不能 expresses inability or prohibition, not the English imperative “Don't rely.”

column2: Something wrong?
column4: “不行吗？”是在问某事是否不可以；“Something wrong?”是在问是否出了问题。

column1: 不要做评判，这样您自己才不会被人评判。
column2: Don't judge and you won't be judged.
column4: “做评判” is unnatural here; say “不要评判” or “不要论断”.

column2: Don't be late for school again.
column4: “不要再上学迟到了” is not a natural word order. Say “上学不要再迟到”.

column2: Not again!
column4: “不要再来一次了” means “Don’t do it again,” not “Not again!”

column2: If you hear hoofbeats, don't look for zebras.
column4: The Chinese means not to believe something just because you heard it; the English idiom means not to assume an unusual explanation when an ordinary one is likely.

column1: 不要忘记你终会有死去的一天。
column2: Keep in mind that you must die.
column4: “你终会有死去的一天” is unnatural; a native speaker would say “你终有一天会死.”

column2: Don't be so pessimistic.
column4: “不要感觉那么悲观” sounds unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “别这么悲观”.

column1: 不要把个人行为上升到集体。
column2: Don't generalize individual behavior to an entire group.
column4: “上升到集体” is an unnatural construction here; say “上升到集体层面”.

column2: Don't pull my leg!
column4: “拉我的腿” is a literal, unnatural rendering of the idiom “pull my leg.”

column1: 不要生气，我又不是故意的。
column2: Don't be mad.It really wasn't on purpose.
column4: There is no space after the period in “Don't be mad.It”.

column1: 不要相信一个你一点都不了解他过去的人。
column2: Don't trust a man whose past you know nothing about.
column4: “他” is awkwardly redundant in the relative clause. A natural version is “不要相信一个你对他的过去一点都不了解的人。”

column2: Don't walk across the tracks!
column4: “翻越铁轨” is not a natural way to say “walk across the tracks”; use “穿越” or “横穿铁轨.”

column2: Don't hold your rival cheap.
column4: “Hold your rival cheap” is not a natural way to say this; use “underestimate your rival.”

column1: 与其知道你要走，我宁肯你没有回来过。
column2: I would rather that you never returned than know that you wanted to leave.
column4: “宁肯你没有回来过” is unnatural here; a native speaker would more naturally say “我宁愿你从来没有回来过.”

column1: 与汽车相比，我更喜欢坐火车。
column2: Comparing with cars, I prefer taking the train.
column4: “Comparing with cars” is ungrammatical here; say “Compared with cars” or “Compared to driving, I prefer taking the train.”

column1: 世事变幻无常，人不能因循守旧、一成不变。
column2: Things change from time to time, and one should change with them.
column4: The Chinese says people should not cling to old ways or remain unchanged; that point is missing from the English.

column1: 世界上阴阳人比犹太人数量还多。
column2: There are more intersex people in the world than there are Jewish people.
column4: “阴阳人” is a derogatory or misleading term here; “双性人” is the neutral term for intersex people.

column1: 世界人口将在不久的将来增加两倍。
column2: The population of the world will double before long.
column4: “增加两倍” means increase by two times (to three times the original), not double.

column1: 两个房间中间有一面墙。
column2: placeholder-p13
column4: “placeholder-p13” is not an English translation.

column2: two wives
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” does not translate the Chinese sentence.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: The two views oppose.
column4: “The two views oppose” is awkward and incomplete; a natural phrasing is “The two views are opposed.”

column2: 12 o'clock noon
column4: This is a time fragment, not a sentence.

column2: China developed very quickly.
column4: The Chinese describes China’s development in the present or generally, while the English says it developed in the past.

column1: 中国的历史爸爸什么都知道。
column2: My dad knows everything about Chinese history.
column4: The word order is unnatural; say “爸爸对中国的历史什么都知道” or “爸爸什么都知道中国的历史.”

column2: For his ideal, he keeps striving.
column4: “For his ideal” is unnatural English; “for his ideals” or “in pursuit of his ideal” would be more natural.

column1: 为了解决问题，他们尽了很大努力。
column2: They made a great effort to settle the problem.
column4: “尽了很大努力” is unnatural; say “付出了很大努力” or “做了很大努力”.

column1: 为什么你想到外国读书？
column2: Why do you want to study abroad?
column4: “想到外国读书” is unnatural here; a natural phrasing is “为什么你想去外国读书？”

column1: 为什么你星期六来不了？
column2: Why couldn't you come on Saturday?
column4: “来不了” means “can’t come,” not “couldn’t come.”

column2: Why did you use up all the money?
column4: “花了所有钱”不自然；通常说“花了所有的钱”或“把钱都花光了”。

column1: 为什么您想到外国读书？
column2: Why do you want to study abroad?
column4: “想到外国读书”不自然；通常说“想去国外读书”。

column2: Why do I have to go to school?
column4: “应该” means “should,” while “have to” expresses necessity.

column2: Why are the police here?
column4: “为什么这有警察” is unnatural Chinese. Say “为什么这里有警察？”

column2: A toast to our friendship!
column4: “为我们的友好干杯” sounds unnatural; “为我们的友谊干杯” is the natural phrasing.

column2: To make an excuse for having stayed out late.
column4: Both sides are fragments rather than complete sentences.

column2: And after?
column4: “And after?” is not a natural way to ask what happened next; “And then?” would be natural.

column2: 9 o'clock
column4: This is a time fragment, not a sentence.

column2: Actually.
column4: “事实上。” / “Actually.” are fragments rather than complete sentences.

column1: 二十美金等于一百四十元。
column2: Twenty dollars are one hundred and forty yuan.
column4: “Twenty dollars are” is ungrammatical here; say “Twenty dollars is equal to…”

column1: 二手车比新车便宜得多。
column2: Used cars are much cheaper.
column4: The Chinese explicitly says used cars are cheaper than new cars; the English omits that comparison.

column2: Know each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Hurt each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Use each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Respect each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Help each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Influence each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Support each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Encourage each other
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: five weeks
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.
This is a time phrase, not a sentence.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: Five hundred years ago it was a house.
column4: “一家” means one family or household, not “a house.”

column2: The total output is large.
column4: “总量” means total quantity; “total output” specifically refers to production.

column1: 人们说得好，音乐是天使的话语。
column2: Music is well said to be the speech of angels.
column4: “人们说得好” is unnatural here; “人们常说” would fit.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” does not translate the Chinese sentence.

column2: People come and go a lot.
column4: “人来人往” already describes people coming and going; “出入很多” is awkward here.

column2: Every man is a potential corpse.
column4: The Chinese says people may die at any time; it does not say every man is a potential corpse.

column2: What's the happy occasion?
column4: The Chinese asks what is making someone so happy, not what the occasion is.

column2: What's so fucking funny?
column4: The word order is unnatural; a native speaker would phrase this differently.

column1: 什么意思，他竟然一直在欺骗我！
column2: I ask you, he's been cheating me!
column4: 什么意思想的是“What do you mean?”; “I ask you” does not convey that meaning.

column1: 什么都不要做比做错了好。
column2: It's better to do nothing than to do something poorly.
column4: “做错了” means doing something wrong, not merely doing it poorly.

column2: 4:30 p.m. this afternoon.
column4: This is a time fragment, not a sentence.

column1: 今天下这么大的雨，土松着呢。
column2: It is still raining a lot today, and the soil is being broken up.
column4: 土松着呢 means the soil is loose, not that it is being broken up.

column1: 今天天气不错，出去走走吧。
column2: The weather is excellent today. Go for a walk.
column4: The Chinese suggests that we go for a walk together, while the English is an instruction to the listener.

column2: The sun is strong today.
column4: “The sun is strong today” is unnatural English; “It’s very sunny today” is more natural.

column1: 今天早上，我吃了面包夹黄油。
column2: I ate bread and butter this morning.
column4: “面包夹黄油”不太自然；通常说“抹了黄油的面包”或“面包抹黄油”。

column1: 今天晚上老板要和我们一起加班。
column2: Tonight the boss is going to to work overtime together with us.
column4: “Going to to work” has an extra “to.”

column2: It's insanely hot today.
column4: “今天疯狂的热”不自然；可以说“今天热得疯狂”或“今天热疯了”。

column2: Today is awful, raining nonstop.
column4: “Today is awful, raining nonstop” is awkward and ungrammatical; say “Today is awful; it’s been raining nonstop.”

column1: 今天这么热，你还出门吗？
column2: It's so hot today, yet you're going out now?
column4: The Chinese asks whether the person will still go out; the English sounds like it assumes they are going out.

column2: I am going to France in Summer this Year.
column4: The capitalization is incorrect; it should be “this summer” and “this year.”

column1: 今日的生活是迅息万变和复杂的。
column2: Life today is fast-moving and complex.
column4: “迅息万变” contains a wrong character; the expression is “瞬息万变”。

column2: from 2004 to 2008
column4: This is a date range, not a complete sentence.

column1: 从一号到五号都在下雨。
column2: From the first to the fifth, it's been raining non-stop.
column4: 都在下雨 means it was raining throughout the period or on each day, not necessarily non-stop.

column1: 从南京西路到南京东路
column2: from West Nanjing Road to East Nanjing Road
column4: This is a route phrase, not a complete sentence.

column1: 从天色看起来，下午可能会下雨。
column2: From the look of the sky, it may rain in the afternoon.
column4: “从天色看起来” is unnatural; say “从天色来看” or “看天色”.

column2: Overall, great progress.
column4: “Overall, great progress” is a sentence fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column1: 从此他养成了写日记的习惯。
column2: From then on he kept a diary.
column4: The Chinese says he developed the habit of keeping a diary, which the English leaves out.

column1: 从这个层面看，他是对的。
column2: From this level, he's right.
column4: “From this level” is unnatural here; say “From this perspective” or “In this respect.”

column1: 从这儿到那儿是很近的。
column2: It's not far from here to there.
column4: “从这儿到那儿很近” is the natural phrasing; “是很近的” is awkward here.

column1: 从这里步行到你家要多长时间？
column2: How long does it take from here to your house on foot?
column4: The English is missing “to get”: say “How long does it take to get from here to your house on foot?”

column1: 从那天起我一直在等他。
column2: I am still waiting for him since that day.
column4: “I am still waiting for him since that day” is ungrammatical; use “I have been waiting for him since that day.”

column1: 他/她的大衣内衬是用皮毛做的。
column2: Her coat is fur on the inside.
column4: The Chinese says “his/her,” while the English specifies “her.”

column2: He has gone abroad by himself.
column4: The Chinese says he went abroad alone; the English says he has gone abroad alone.

column1: 他一个人在外地，没法儿照顾家。
column2: Alone away, he can't care for family.
column4: “Alone away” is unnatural English; the sentence should say he is alone away from home or living elsewhere.

column2: He thanked us repeatedly.
column4: The Chinese says he repeatedly expressed thanks, but the English adds that he thanked “us.”

column2: He has been absent from work for a week.
column4: “来工作” is not a natural way to say someone has been absent from work; “一周没来上班了” would be more idiomatic.

column1: 他一生为急性疼痛所苦。
column2: He's suffering from acute pain in his life.
column4: “He's suffering from acute pain in his life” is unnatural English; it does not naturally convey that he suffered throughout his life.

column1: 他一面开车一面听收音机的音乐。
column2: He drove the car, listening to music on the radio.
column4: “收音机的音乐” is unnatural here; say “收音机里的音乐.”

column2: He had elementary education.
column4: “上的是初等教育” is not natural Mandarin; say “接受的是初等教育” or “上的是初等学校”。

column1: 他不仅有学识还有经验。
column2: He has not only learning but experience.
column4: “Not only learning but experience” is awkward and unidiomatic; “not only knowledge but also experience” is natural.

column2: He couldn't go against his principles.
column4: 不会 means “won’t” or “can’t,” not “couldn’t.”

column2: He is careless about money.
column4: “他不关心钱” means he doesn’t care about money, not that he is careless with it.

column1: 他不开门，所以她没办法进去。
column2: He didn't open the door, so she has no way to enter.
column4: 不开门 means “doesn’t/won’t open the door,” not “didn’t open the door.”

column1: 他不想要任何种类的花。
column2: He wants no kind of flowers.
column4: “不想要任何种类的花” is unnatural; a native speaker would say “他什么花都不想要”.

column2: He didn't know that.
column4: 他不知道 means “he doesn’t know” or “he didn’t know”; it does not specify “that.”

column2: He could not swim.
column4: “他不能游泳” means he cannot swim, not that he could not swim in the past.

column2: He couldn't remember my address.
column4: The Chinese says he no longer remembers the address, while the English says he couldn't remember it at a past time.

column2: He paints in his spare time.
column4: 学画画 means learning to paint, not necessarily painting in his spare time.

column2: He gave her everything.
column4: “为她做了一切” means he did everything for her, not that he gave her everything.

column2: He was killed by my hand.
column4: “他为我亲手所杀”不自然；可说“他是被我亲手杀死的”。

column2: He clipped the sheep.
column4: 为羊只修剪羊毛 is unnatural here; a natural phrasing is 他给羊剪毛。

column2: He bought a disc set.
column4: 一集 is not a natural classifier for a disc set; use 一套光盘.

column1: 他买了新衣服给他的女儿。
column2: He bought his daughter a new dress.
column4: 新衣服 means new clothes, not specifically a new dress.

column2: He'll be back by five o'clock.
column4: 五点左右 means around five, not necessarily by five.

column1: 他今年的年龄是三十岁。
column2: His age this year is thirty.
column4: “今年的年龄”表达累赘且不自然，通常说“他今年三十岁”。

column2: He works in arts.
column4: “He works in arts” is unnatural English; say “He works in the arts.”

column2: He works from morning until night.
column4: “从早工作到晚” is unnatural; a natural phrasing is “从早到晚工作。”

column1: 他从没见过那么坏的男孩。
column2: He had never seen such a bad boy.
column4: 中文“从没见过”表达从未有过这种经历，英文过去完成时“had never seen”需要一个过去参照点。

column1: 他以总统的身份访问了日本。
column2: He visited Japan in the character of President.
column4: “In the character of President”不是自然的英语表达；可说“in his capacity as president”。

column2: They were always making jokes.
column4: “闹笑话”是出洋相或闹出笑话，不是“making jokes”。

column1: 他们不想要孩子。还有，他们也没时间照顾孩子。
column2: They don't want to have kids. Plus, they wouldn't have time to look after a kid.
column4: “没时间” says they don't have time; “wouldn't have time” adds a hypothetical meaning.

column1: 他们从去年开始学英文。
column2: They started studying English last year.
column4: “从去年开始学” suggests they have been studying since last year, not merely that they started then.

column1: 他们以前没有钱，可是很快乐。
column2: They didn't have much money before, but they were happy.
column4: 没有钱 means they had no money, not merely that they didn't have much money.

column2: Their company is in Bejing.
column4: “Bejing” is misspelled; it should be “Beijing.”

column1: 他们向我保证没有任何物品剩下。
column2: They confirmed to me that there weren't any goods left.
column4: “保证” means assure or guarantee, not simply confirm.

column2: We're buying movie tickets.
column4: The Chinese says “they,” but the English says “we.”

column1: 他们在酒吧待了一个晚上了。
column2: They have been staying at the bar for the whole evening.
column4: “一个晚上” means all night, not just the whole evening.

column2: They went to the station by car.
column4: 坐车 means traveling by vehicle; it does not specifically say they went by car.

column1: 他们对他们的员工保证就业。
column2: They guaranteed regular employment to their workers.
column4: “对员工保证就业” is unnatural; a more natural phrasing is “向员工保证就业”.

column1: 他们已经两天没吃东西了。
column2: They haven't eating anything for two days already.
column4: “Haven't eating” is ungrammatical; say “haven't eaten.”

column1: 他们扩阔了帝国的领土。
column2: They increased the territory of the empire.
column4: “扩阔领土” is an unnatural collocation; “扩大领土” is natural.

column2: They are one generation.
column4: “They are one generation” is unnatural English; say “They belong to the same generation.”

column2: They have.
column4: 他们有 / They have is incomplete without context specifying what they have.

column2: They were girding for the exam.
column4: “Girding for the exam” is an unnatural way to say they were preparing for an exam.

column2: They eat meat once a week.
column4: “尝一次肉” means to taste meat once, not to eat meat once a week.

column2: their stuff
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: Her daughter is a nurse.
column4: 他们的女儿 means “their daughter,” not “her daughter.”

column1: 他们的损失到达了一百万日圆。
column2: Their losses reached one million yen.
column4: “损失到达了一百万”不自然；可说“损失达到了一百万日圆”。

column1: 他们签了合约，避免了战争。
column2: They signed a treaty and avoided war.
column4: 合约通常指 contract; treaty is more naturally 条约 here.

column2: They don't pay me enough.
column4: 没给够 says they did not give enough, while the English describes an ongoing pay situation.

column1: 他们认为当时是采取行动的最好时机。
column2: They decided it was a perfect time to make the move.
column4: 认为 means “thought/considered,” not “decided.”

column2: They said no.
column4: 他们说了不 is not a natural way to say “They said no.”

column1: 他们说他是一个很能干的人。
column2: They say that he is an able man.
column4: “An able man” is an unnatural way to express that he is capable.

column1: 他们这么热情的欢迎我，让我感觉家人一样。
column2: They welcomed me warmly, so I felt at home.
column4: “让我感觉家人一样” is unnatural; it should say “让我感觉像家人一样” or “让我有家的感觉”.

column2: They all loved it.
column4: “他们都很喜欢” leaves what they like unstated, so it needs context that is not provided.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: Will he tell me the truth?
column4: “真想” means true thoughts or real wishes; “the truth” is “真相”.

column2: He can play the instrument.
column4: “The instrument” implies a specific instrument, while the Chinese just says he can play an instrument.

column2: He hurt his left hand.
column4: “伤害” is unnatural for injuring a hand; say “他弄伤了左手” or “他伤了左手”.

column2: He lives nearby to my house.
column4: “Nearby to my house” is unidiomatic; say “near my house” or “nearby.”

column2: He lived in Matsue for seven years.
column4: “住在……七年了” means he has lived there for seven years and still lives there; “He lived” suggests he no longer does.

column2: He did much investigation.
column4: “Did much investigation” is unnatural; say “did a lot of research” or “conducted many surveys.”

column2: He works down-to-earth.
column4: “Works down-to-earth” is ungrammatical; say “He works in a down-to-earth manner” or “He is practical in his work.”

column2: He did it on the sly.
column4: This is an elliptical fragment; without context, it does not stand as a complete sentence.

column2: He stored much data.
column4: “Much data” is unnatural here; “a lot of data” is the natural phrasing.

column2: She's like her mum.
column4: The Chinese says “he,” but the English says “she.”

column2: All his family works on a farm.
column4: “All his family works” is awkward; a natural phrasing is “His whole family works on a farm.”

column2: He is leaving the house at 8 o'clock.
column4: The Chinese describes a regular action; the English describes a specific upcoming departure.

column2: He could no longer contain his anger.
column4: “忍不住气” is not a natural expression here; “忍不住生气” or “忍不下这口气” would be natural.

column2: He posted a notice.
column4: “写了一个启事” means he wrote a notice, not necessarily that he posted it.

column2: the books that he wrote
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: He's writing a long letter.
column4: 他写长信 describes writing long letters habitually; it does not say he is writing one now.

column1: 他动不动就发脾气，所以人人都怕了他。
column2: He loses his temper so easily that everybody avoids him.
column4: “怕了他” means everyone was afraid of him; it does not say they avoid him.

column2: He wasn't given any reward for his service.
column4: “他劳无所获” is not a grammatical or idiomatic expression; it should be something like“他劳而无获”。

column2: He advanced to high school.
column4: “升学到了高中”不自然；通常说“升入高中”或“考上高中”。

column2: He went to the interior to work.
column4: 内地 generally means the mainland, not “the interior.”

column2: He went several times.
column4: “好几番” is not a natural way to say “several times”; use “好几次”.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: He takes makeup classes at a cram school.
column4: “补课” means taking extra or remedial lessons, not necessarily makeup classes.

column2: He goes to refund the ticket.
column4: “He goes to refund the ticket” is unnatural English; say “He goes to get a refund for the ticket.”

column1: 他去那个中国饭馆吃饭了。
column2: He is going to that Chinese restaurant to eat a meal.
column4: “他去……了” describes having gone, not that he is going.

column2: He checks the account at the bank.
column4: The Chinese says he goes to the bank to check the account; the English says he checks it there, without the going.

column2: He collects the bonus.
column4: “他去领取奖金” says he went or is going to collect the bonus, not that he collects it as a general or present action.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: He joined the contest.
column4: “赛”不能单独这样使用；应说“参加了比赛”。

column2: He talked with his eyes shining.
column4: “说著” mixes simplified and traditional characters; in simplified Chinese, write “说着.”

column2: He asked me back.
column4: “Asked me back” is not a natural way to express this.

column2: He got a very good score.
column4: “取得了很好的分数” is an awkward collocation; “取得了很好的成绩” or “得了很高的分数” is more natural.

column2: He is loved by his people.
column4: “他的人民” would mean “his people”; the Chinese just says “the people.”

column1: 他受伤的脚又开始流血了。
column2: His wounded leg began to bleed again.
column4: 脚 means “foot,” not “leg.”

column2: He might have lost his way.
column4: “他可能已经迷失了”听起来不完整；表达“lost his way”通常说“他可能已经迷路了”。

column2: He called on all to save.
column4: “Called on all to save” is awkward; “called on everyone to economize” is more natural.

column2: He sighed it's too hard.
column4: The reported speech is ungrammatical; say “He sighed and said it was too hard.”

column2: He ate one apple.
column4: “一颗苹果” is not the natural measure phrase; say “一个苹果.”

column2: He eats too much.
column4: “吃得过于多” is unnatural; say “吃得太多.”

column1: 他听到这个消息非常喜欢。
column2: He became very elated at the news.
column4: “听到这个消息非常喜欢” is unnatural here; say “听到这个消息非常高兴” or “听到这个消息很兴奋”。

column2: He stayed home all day.
column4: “All day” is added in the English but not stated in the Chinese.

column2: He came with his brother.
column4: 中文说他和妈妈一起来，英文却说他和兄弟一起来。

column1: 他和老板有矛盾，这个我们知道就好。
column2: Between you and me, he's in trouble with the boss.
column4: “有矛盾” says he and his boss have a conflict, not simply that he is in trouble with the boss.

column1: 他和许多其他人一样问了我同样的问题。
column2: He asked me questions similar to those asked by many others.
column4: The Chinese says he asked the same question as many other people; the English says he asked questions similar to theirs.

column2: He loves sports events.
column4: “体育活动”指体育运动或体育锻炼，不特指体育赛事。

column2: He drinks too much and became a drunkard.
column4: “He drinks” and “became” have inconsistent tenses.

column2: He drinks alcohol; I drink juice.
column4: “喝酒水” is not a natural way to say that he drinks alcohol.

column1: 他喝酒醉得无法开车回家。
column2: He is too drunk to drive home.
column4: “喝酒醉得” is not natural Mandarin; say “他喝醉了，无法开车回家”.

column2: He speaks in a dialect.
column4: “他嘴里一口方言” is unnatural; a native speaker would say “他满口方言” or “他说一口方言.”

column1: 他因为准备太少考试不及格了。
column2: He failed in the examination for lack of preparation.
column4: “准备太少”在这里说法不自然；应说“准备得太少”。

column1: 他在五年前，也就是十二岁的时候来了东京。
column2: He came to Tokyo five years ago, that is to say, when he was twelve years old.
column4: “来了东京” is unnatural; say “来到东京” or “来东京.”

column1: 他在仅仅是在一旁旁观，而没有去阻止争吵。
column2: He just looked on and didn't stop the quarrel.
column4: “在仅仅是在” is an obvious repetition; the sentence should be “他仅仅是在一旁旁观……”.

column2: He sees internal medicine.
column4: “He sees internal medicine” is not natural English; he sees a doctor in the internal medicine department.

column2: He is in his library.
column4: 中文只说他在图书馆里，没有说那是他的图书馆；英文增加了所属关系。

column2: He sees the surgery department.
column4: “He sees the surgery department” is unnatural English for receiving medical care there.

column2: He stayed in bed.
column4: 中文说他正躺在床上，英文说他待在床上。

column2: He is towing.
column4: “他在拖” leaves out what he is towing or dragging, so it needs context.

column2: He is first on the chart.
column4: “他在排行榜上第一” is unnatural; say “他在排行榜上排名第一”.

column2: He stayed here two days.
column4: The English needs “for”: “He stayed here for two days.”

column1: 他在银行里有大量钱财。
column2: He has a lot of money in the bank.
column4: “在银行里有大量钱财” is unnatural; “在银行里有很多钱” or “有大量存款” would be more idiomatic.

column2: He goes abroad by plane.
column4: “去外国” is unnatural here; a native speaker would usually say “去国外” or “去别的国家”.

column2: He works out; great physique.
column4: “Great physique” is a fragment; the English should say that he has a great physique.

column2: He lost his job but not hope.
column4: “没有失望” means “was not disappointed,” not “did not lose hope.”

column2: He has a headache; sees a doctor.
column4: “He has a headache; sees a doctor” is ungrammatical; the second clause needs a subject, such as “he sees a doctor.”

column2: He rose in resistance.
column4: “Rose in resistance” is not natural English.

column2: He seems like he doesn't understand this at all.
column4: “知清” is incorrect here; the phrase should be “知情” or, more naturally, “清楚”.

column2: Fuck you!
column4: 他妈的 is an expletive like “damn it,” not “fuck you.”

column2: He'd prefer not to eat that.
column4: 中文说“不吃这个”（this），英文却说“不吃那个”（that）。

column2: He teaches English to his friend.
column4: “对他的朋友教英语” is unnatural; say “教他的朋友英语”.

column2: He will work in another city.
column4: “外地” means another place, not specifically another city.

column2: He commands the respect of a king.
column4: “尊贵如国王” describes him as as noble or revered as a king; it does not say he commands a king’s respect.

column2: He is precisely our coach.
column4: “Precisely our coach” is an unnatural way to express this; “He is our coach” is more natural.

column2: That con man is him!
column4: “That con man is him” is awkward English; a natural translation is “He is that con man” or “That’s the con man.”

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” does not translate the Chinese sentence.

column1: 他工作很主动，也很自觉。
column2: He works proactively and self-consciously.
column4: “自觉” here means conscientious or self-disciplined, not “self-consciously.”

column2: He almost froze to death from the snow.
column4: “Froze to death from the snow” is unnatural here; “in the snow” would be natural.

column1: 他已经不再是以前那个快乐的男孩了。
column2: He is not the cheerful man he was.
column4: 中文说的是“男孩”，英文说的是“man”。

column1: 他已经不是我最初见他那时的那个人了。
column2: He is not the man that he was when I first knew him.
column4: “见他”是见到他或初次见面，不等于英文的“first knew him”。

column1: 他年纪够大可以了解它。
column2: He is old enough to understand it.
column4: 年纪够大可以了解它 is awkward; a more natural phrasing would be 年纪够大，能理解它.

column2: He moved the desk to the right.
column4: The word order is unnatural; a native speaker would say “他把书桌往右边移了”.

column1: 他很会教育人，所以他的孩子都很听话。
column2: He was a great teacher so his children were very obedient.
column4: The Chinese describes him in the present, while the English says he was a great teacher.

column2: He's very forgetful of things.
column4: “Forgetful of things” is unnatural; say “He’s very forgetful.”

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder”不是这句话的英文翻译。

column2: He'll be done soon.
column4: 很快就好了 means he’ll be better or okay soon, not that he’ll be done soon.

column2: placeholder
column4: “很有职责” is unnatural; “很有责任心” would be more idiomatic.

column1: 他很民主，听大家的意见。
column2: He is democratic, heeding all.
column4: “Heeding all” is awkward and incomplete; it should say he listens to everyone’s opinions.

column2: He was very old.
column4: The Chinese says he is old, while the English says he was old.

column2: He is lazy and does nothing.
column4: “赖” does not mean “lazy” here; the usual character is “懒.”

column2: He can scarcely write his name.
column4: 很难写 means it is difficult for him to write his name, not that he can scarcely write it.

column2: He acknowledged his faults.
column4: 得知了他的错误 means he learned or found out about his mistake, not that he acknowledged his faults.

column2: He has a lot on his mind to say.
column4: “A lot on his mind to say” is awkward English; a natural phrasing is “He has a lot he wants to say.”

column2: That person needs to be relieved from his post.
column4: “Relieved from his post” is unnatural; say “relieved of his post” or “removed from his position.”

column2: He almost died.
column4: 他快死了 means he is about to die, not that he almost died.

column1: 他怎么在这样的贫困中谋生？
column2: How did he make his living in such poverty?
column4: The Chinese asks how he makes a living, while the English asks how he made a living in the past.

column2: He would like to buy a big apartment.
column4: “房子” means a house/home or dwelling in general; it does not specifically mean an apartment.

column2: He wants a book to read.
column4: 找本书 means looking for/finding a book; the English only says he wants a book to read.

column2: Nothing is going his way.
column4: The Chinese says that what he thinks of or hopes for will not come true; the English says things are not going his way.

column2: He was willing to work for others.
column4: The Chinese says he is willing to work for others, while the English says he was willing.

column2: He wears glasses.
column4: The usual measure word is 副: 他戴着一副眼镜.

column2: What he said is all fact.
column4: “All fact” is ungrammatical here; say “all facts” or “all factual.”

column2: He interrupted our discussion.
column4: “打断我们的谈论”不自然；“打断我们的讨论”更常见。

column2: He plays ball wonderfully.
column4: “Plays ball wonderfully” is unnatural English; say “He plays sports very well” or name the sport.

column2: He intends to return to the country earlier.
column4: “Return to the country earlier” is unnatural English; “return to the country early” would be more natural.

column2: He helps the elder cross the road.
column4: “The elder” is not natural here; say “the elderly person” or “an old person.”

column2: He mixed the two waters.
column4: “The two waters” is unnatural in English; “the two types of water” would be clearer.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: He tucked the book under his arm.
column4: 把书夹在手里 means holding or pinching the book in one's hand, not tucking it under one's arm.

column1: 他把他的一生献给了他的国家。
column2: He gave his life for his country.
column4: 献给了一生 means he devoted his life to his country, not that he died for it.

column1: 他把全副心神放在学业上。
column2: He applied himself to his study.
column4: “His study” is unnatural here; “his studies” would be more natural.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column1: 他把自己的钱包掉到地上，现在是我的了。
column2: He dropped his wallet, and now it's mine.
column4: “把自己的钱包掉到地上” is not natural phrasing here; use “把自己的钱包掉在地上” or “把自己的钱包弄掉到地上.”

column1: 他把赚到的钱都存了起来。
column2: He saves what he earns.
column4: The Chinese says he saved all the money he earned, while the English describes a habitual action.

column1: 他把问题从脑子里排除了。
column2: He cast off the problem from his mind.
column4: “把问题从脑子里排除了” is not a natural way to express putting a problem out of one’s mind.

column2: He raised his head at me.
column4: “Raised his head at me” is awkward and does not naturally express looking at someone.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not an English translation.

column2: He zipped his bag shut.
column4: “拉上了他的包” is not a natural way to say he zipped his bag shut; say “拉上了包的拉链” or “把包拉上了.”

column2: He caught my hand and pulled me to the second floor.
column4: The English adds that he caught the speaker’s hand, which the Chinese does not say.

column2: He rejected our offer.
column4: “邀请” means invitation, while “offer” means an offer.

column2: He owns much wealth.
column4: “Owns much wealth” is awkward; “owns a lot of wealth” is more natural.

column2: He took it literally.
column4: This is an incomplete phrase; it needs a verb to form a natural sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not an English translation.

column1: 他探索一切逃走的可能性。
column2: He is exploring the possibility of all escapes.
column4: “the possibility of all escapes” is garbled; the meaning is that he is exploring every possibility of escaping.

column1: 他推着轮椅和奶奶散步。
column2: He pushes grandma's wheelchair on walks.
column4: 中文只说他推着轮椅和奶奶散步，没有说明奶奶坐在轮椅里；英文明确说是奶奶的轮椅。

column2: He mentioned a problem.
column4: “提了个问题” means “raised/asked a question,” not “mentioned a problem.”

column1: 他提出了几个改变事物的方法。
column2: He gave several examples of how we could change things.
column4: The Chinese says he proposed several methods, while the English says he gave examples.

column2: He's moved away.
column4: “搬了家” means he moved house; it doesn’t necessarily mean he moved away.

column2: He broke up the chair for firewood.
column4: “摔断了椅子当柴火” is not a natural way to say he broke up a chair to use as firewood.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not an English translation of the Chinese sentence.

column1: 他整天整整忙了十二个小时。
column2: He was busy a full twelve hours all day.
column4: “整天” and “整整十二个小时” are redundant and make the sentence sound unnatural.

column2: He looks aslant.
column4: “他斜着身子看” means he leans his body to look, not that he looks sideways or aslant.

column1: 他是个富有才能的年轻导演。
column2: He's a talented young director.
column4: “富有才能” is unnatural here; “很有才能” or “很有才华” is more natural.

column2: What he says always corresponds with what he does.
column4: 表里如一 means being consistent inside and out; it does not specifically say that his words always match his actions.

column1: 他是公司的股东和首席。
column2: He is a shareholder and chief.
column4: “首席” is awkward and incomplete as a standalone description here.

column2: He is the scholar in our class.
column4: “我们班里的秀才” sounds unnatural in modern Mandarin; 秀才 usually refers to a historical degree-holder.

column1: 他是我其中一个最要好的朋友。
column2: He is one of my best friends.
column4: “我其中一个最要好的朋友” is unnatural word order; say “我最要好的朋友之一” or “我的其中一位好朋友”.

column2: He is a chess expert.
column4: “打球” refers to playing ball games, not chess.

column2: He wrote the letter with a fountain pen.
column4: “他是用钢笔写的信” is malformed for the intended meaning. Say“他是用钢笔写的这封信” or“他用钢笔写了这封信”。

column1: 他是运动会的冠军，我是亚军。
column2: He is the champion; I'm runner-up.
column4: “I’m runner-up” is missing an article; it should be “I’m the runner-up.”

column1: 他是这次纠纷的凶手吗？
column2: Is he the culprit in this dispute?
column4: “凶手”通常指杀人者，用来指纠纷中的责任人或罪魁祸首不自然。

column2: He hinted for me to stay quiet.
column4: “Hinted for me to” is ungrammatical; say “hinted that I should stay quiet.”

column1: 他更愿意工作而不是无所事事。
column2: He preferred working to doing nothing.
column4: The Chinese expresses a present preference; the English says he preferred it in the past.

column2: He had a daughter.
column4: 他有 means “he has,” not “he had.”

column2: He has three brothers.
column4: 兄长 specifically means older brothers; the English does not specify that they are older.

column1: 他有些在日本不能找到的外书。
column2: He has some foreign books that cannot be found in Japan.
column4: “外书” is not a natural way to say “foreign books”; use “外国书” or “外国书籍.”

column2: Does he hope to succeed?
column4: The Chinese asks whether he has a chance of succeeding; the English asks whether he hopes to succeed.

column2: He had a lot of work to do.
column4: 有 means “has”; the English says “had.”

column2: He has much money.
column4: “He has much money” is unnatural in affirmative English; “He has a lot of money” is natural.

column2: He has great authority.
column4: “有很大的权” is unnatural; say “有很大的权力” or “有很大的权威”。

column2: He has a strong sense of self.
column4: “他有很强的自我” is not a natural way to express having a strong sense of self.

column2: He has high quality.
column4: “Has high quality” is unnatural for a person; say “has high caliber” or “is of high quality.”

column2: He wrote to me from time to time.
column4: The Chinese describes a habitual action, while the English puts it in the past.

column2: He has rich experience.
column4: “Rich experience” is an unnatural collocation in English; say “extensive experience.”

column1: 他有能力比我做得更好。
column2: He can do it better than I can.
column4: 语序不自然；可说“他有能力做得比我更好”。

column2: He came into my room.
column4: “他来了我的房间” is not natural Mandarin for “He came into my room.” Say “他来到我的房间” or “他进了我的房间。”

column2: He came just in time.
column4: “来得恰恰是时候” is awkward; a native speaker would more naturally say “来得正是时候” or “来得恰好是时候”.

column2: He loves sports intensely.
column4: “Loves sports intensely” is unnatural English.

column2: He was listening to music.
column4: “正在听” describes an action happening now, while “was listening” places it in the past.

column1: 他正遭受严重头痛的困扰。
column2: He was suffering from a bad headache.
column4: “遭受严重头痛的困扰”表达生硬；可以说“他正受严重头痛困扰”。

column1: 他每件事做之前都会细心计划。
column2: He always plans a thing out carefully before he does it.
column4: “Plans a thing out” is unnatural English; “carefully plans everything” would be more idiomatic.

column2: He doesn't listen.
column4: “他没听”表示他没有听（某次），英文“doesn't listen”表示习惯上不听。

column2: He wasn't able to open the box.
column4: The Chinese describes lacking the ability to open the box, while the English specifically says he wasn't able to, suggesting a past inability.

column2: He is able to swim quickly.
column4: The Chinese says he swims very fast, not that he is able to swim quickly.

column2: He loved to laugh and enjoy life.
column4: “爱欢笑与享受生活”搭配生硬，不是自然的中文表达。

column2: He particularly liked history.
column4: 特别的喜欢 is incorrect here; say 特别喜欢 or 特别地喜欢.

column2: He came specially to see me.
column4: “Came specially to see me” is unnatural; “came especially to see me” is more natural.

column2: He specially cooked.
column4: “He specially cooked” is unnatural; “He made a meal especially for the occasion” is more natural.

column1: 他现在火得不得了，每个人都知道他。
column2: He's terribly hot right now. Everyone knows him.
column4: Here 火 means popular or famous, not physically or figuratively “hot” as in the English.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not an English translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: He filled the bottle with water.
column4: The phrasing is unnatural; say “他把瓶子装满了水” or “他用水把瓶子装满了.”

column2: His works are full of ideas.
column4: “作品充满了想法” is unnatural; “充满了创意” or “充满了思想” would be more idiomatic.

column2: His accent!
column4: This is a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column2: His brother studies hard.
column4: 很认真学习 is awkward here; say 他学习很认真 or 他很认真地学习.

column1: 他的学问很深，学术水平很高。
column2: He is deeply learned with high academic level.
column4: “With high academic level” is awkward and ungrammatical; say “with a high level of academic ability.”

column1: 他的小说风行了一段长时间。
column2: His novel had a great vogue for a long time.
column4: “一段长时间” is unnatural here; say “很长一段时间”.

column2: His brother studies hard.
column4: “很认真学习” is unnatural here; say “学习很认真” or “很认真地学习.”

column2: He has a kind heart.
column4: “他的心很好” is not a natural way to say he is kind-hearted; “他的心地很好” would be more idiomatic.

column2: He is broad-minded.
column4: “心很宽广” is unnatural here; “心胸很宽广” is idiomatic.

column2: He has a passive character.
column4: “消极” usually means negative or pessimistic, rather than passive.

column2: He had the right idea.
column4: The Chinese says his idea is right, while the English puts it in the past: “had the right idea.”

column1: 他的手指流血了，还好伤不重。
column2: His finger bled, but luckily the injury is light.
column4: “The injury is light” is unnatural English; say “the injury is minor” or “not serious.”

column2: His skills are proficient.
column4: “His skills are proficient” is unidiomatic; a person can be proficient, or their skills can be good.

column2: He is keenly perceptive.
column4: “眼光很敏感” is an unnatural collocation; “观察力敏锐” would be more natural.

column2: His eyes don't feel well.
column4: “His eyes don't feel well” is unnatural English; say “His eyes don't feel right” or “His eyes feel uncomfortable.”

column2: His knowledge is rich.
column4: “His knowledge is rich” is not natural English; say “He has extensive knowledge” or “His knowledge is extensive.”

column2: His pace was slower.
column4: 慢下来了 means his pace slowed down, not simply that it was slower.

column2: He is getting on very well with his English.
column4: “英语很有进步”不自然；通常说“英语进步很大”或“英语有很大进步”。

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: He has a high nose.
column4: “High nose” is not a natural English expression; “prominent nose” would be more idiomatic.

column2: He is not as young as he looks.
column4: “他看上去显老” means he looks old, not that he looks younger than he is.

column1: 他看了她一眼就马上离开了。
column2: With a glance of her, he left swiftly.
column4: “With a glance of her” is unnatural; say “After glancing at her, he left immediately.”

column2: He seemed to be getting thinner every day.
column4: “看来” describes how he seems now, but “seemed” puts it in the past.

column2: He accumulated rich experience.
column4: “Accumulated rich experience” is an unnatural English collocation; “gained extensive experience” is more natural.

column2: He wears a suit.
column4: “穿了一身西装” describes putting on or wearing a suit on a particular occasion, not the habitual “wears a suit.”

column2: He wears cotton clothes.
column4: “棉衣” means a padded cotton coat or jacket, not cotton clothes in general.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column1: 他答应的事情一定会做到。
column2: He always does what he promises.
column4: “一定会做到” means he will certainly do what he promised; “always does” describes a habitual pattern.

column2: He's just lying to you.
column4: “他简直是骗人” is not a natural way to say “He’s just lying to you”; say “他简直是在骗人” or “他简直就是个骗子.”

column2: placeholder
column4: “简直疯狂地高兴” is unnatural; say “高兴得简直要疯了.”

column1: 他终于完成了他的目标。
column2: In the end he achieved his objective.
column4: “完成目标” is an unnatural collocation here; a native speaker would usually say “实现目标” or “达成目标.”

column2: He finally shook off his worries.
column4: “压力” means pressure or stress, not worries.

column2: He will eventually ruin himself.
column4: “自己的” needs a noun here; “毁了自己” would mean “ruin himself.”

column2: He is always online.
column4: 经常 means “often,” not “always.”

column2: He gave her a piece of advice.
column4: 一个忠告 is an unnatural classifier choice here; 一条忠告 is natural.

column1: 他给了我任何我需要的帮助。
column2: He gave me whatever help I needed.
column4: “任何” is unnatural in this affirmative sentence; say “他给了我我需要的所有帮助” or similar.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “给大家很大压迫”说法不自然；可说“给大家很大的压迫感”或“让大家感到很大压力”。

column2: He insured himself.
column4: “给自己投了保险” is unnatural phrasing; say “给自己投保了” or “给自己买了保险。”

column2: His wife.
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: He's definitely somebody clever.
column4: “Somebody clever” is awkward here; “a clever person” is more natural.

column2: He is chubby.
column4: As a predicate, “胖乎乎” sounds incomplete here; say “他胖乎乎的。”

column2: He was able to solve the problem.
column4: The Chinese says he can solve the problem, while the English describes past ability.

column2: He could pass the examination, could not he?
column4: “Could not he?” is not a natural English question tag; “couldn't he?” would be natural.

column2: He is bright.
column4: “他脑子很聪明” is an unnatural way to express that he is intelligent; say “他很聪明” or “他脑子很灵.”

column2: He looks pale; maybe sick.
column4: “Maybe sick” is an incomplete, ungrammatical phrase here; say “maybe he’s sick.”

column2: His leg is in pain.
column4: “他腿疼痛” is unnatural; a native speaker would say “他腿疼” or “他的腿部疼痛”.

column2: He believes himself to be infallible.
column4: “自以为是” means self-righteous or convinced one is right, not infallible.

column2: He self-taught French and Japanese.
column4: “He self-taught” is incorrect here; say “He taught himself French and Japanese.”

column2: It was his own decision.
column4: This is a noun phrase rather than a complete sentence without context.

column1: 他自认为他自己是个伟大的诗人。
column2: He thinks himself a great poet.
column4: 自认为他自己 is awkwardly redundant; say 他自认为是个伟大的诗人。

column1: 他花了一上午的时间看书。
column2: He read a book all morning.
column4: 看书 means reading, without specifying that he read one particular book.

column2: He acted like a madman.
column4: “表现的” should be “表现得” here.

column2: He was harshly criticized.
column4: “严历” is an incorrect character; the phrase should be “严厉批评”.

column2: He was admitted by the company.
column4: “Admitted by the company” is not a natural way to say someone was hired or accepted for a job.

column2: He was made fun of by his classmates.
column4: “欺负”意为bully，而“made fun of”特指嘲笑。

column1: 他被指控犯有好几起侵犯财产罪。
column2: He is charged with multiple property crimes.
column4: “好几起侵犯财产罪” is an unnatural construction; “起” doesn’t fit naturally with “罪” here.

column1: 他被认为是这座城市里最好的律师。
column2: He is reputed the best lawyer in this city.
column4: 应说“He is reputed to be the best lawyer in this city.”

column1: 他要坐早上第一班地铁去上班。
column2: He needs to take the first train in the morning to go to work.
column4: 要坐 means he is going to or wants to take the train; “needs to” adds a sense of necessity.

column2: If he can do that, I will eat my hat.
column4: “他要是成了” means “if he succeeds,” not “if he can do that.”

column2: He wants the money.
column4: “他要钱” means he wants money; it does not specify “the money.”

column2: He untied the rope.
column4: “解开了盒子” means he opened or unfastened the box, not that he untied a rope.

column2: He cleared everyone's doubts.
column4: “解除疑问” is not a natural expression here; say “消除疑问” or “解答疑问.”

column1: 他认真地对我说：“我喜欢你。“
column2: In all seriousness, he said to me: "I like you."
column4: The closing quotation mark is incorrect; it should be ”.

column1: 他让对面的房间都能听到他的声音。
column2: He made himself heard across the room.
column4: 对面的房间 means the room opposite, not across the same room.

column1: 他讲得本来就不对，为什么还要我听他的？
column2: What he says has always been wrong, so why do you still want me to listen to him?
column4: “本来就不对” says what he says is already wrong, not that it has always been wrong.

column2: He speaks English a little.
column4: “He speaks English a little” is awkward; say “He speaks a little English.”

column2: He talks endlessly.
column4: “他说个不止” is not a natural expression; say “他说个不停” for “He talks endlessly.”

column2: He said a piece.
column4: “He said a piece” is not a natural English expression.

column2: He says he'll keep doing that.
column4: The Chinese says he said he would continue; the English says he says he will.

column1: 他说他很生气，还有他要回家吃晚饭了。
column2: He said he was angry, and that he wanted to go home to eat dinner.
column4: “还有他要回家吃晚饭了”接在“他说”后不自然；可说“他说他很生气，还说他要回家吃晚饭了”。

column2: He said he lost his temper.
column4: “生气了” means he became angry; “lost his temper” implies he expressed that anger.

column2: He says he'll correct it.
column4: “能改正” means he can correct it, not necessarily that he will.

column1: 他说的我还是没有全部理解。
column2: I still don't understand everything he says.
column4: The Chinese refers to what he said, while the English refers to what he says.

column1: 他说英文时总要出一点的错。
column2: He never speaks English without making a few mistakes.
column4: “出一点的错” is ungrammatical here. Say “犯一点错” or “出一点错”.

column1: 他说英语流利得就好像他是美国人。
column2: He speaks English so fluently that he resembles an American.
column4: The Chinese says he speaks as fluently as if he were American; the English says his fluency makes him resemble an American.

column1: 他说话夹杂著台湾口音。
column2: He spoke with a Taiwanese accent mixed in.
column4: 夹杂著台湾口音 means his speech was mixed with a Taiwanese accent; the English makes this sound like an accent mixed into something else.

column2: He is speaking quickly.
column4: “他说话很快” describes how he speaks in general, while “He is speaking quickly” describes an ongoing action.

column2: He is wrong, isn't he?
column4: 他说错了 means he said something incorrectly or made a mistake, not simply that he is wrong.

column2: He's read quite a few times.
column4: “He's read quite a few times” sounds incomplete in English; it needs an object, such as “He's read it quite a few times.”

column2: He read a lot.
column4: The Chinese normally means he reads a lot (habitually), while the English says he read a lot (past).

column1: 他调查了两方合作的可能性。
column2: He has investigated the possibility of cooperation.
column4: The Chinese specifies cooperation between two parties, which the English leaves out.

column1: 他跑得能有多快就有多快。
column2: He ran as fast as he could.
column4: “他跑得能有多快就有多快” is not a natural construction. A natural version is “他能跑多快就跑多快.”

column1: 他跟我不住在一个小区。
column2: He doesn't live in my neighborhood.
column4: The word order is awkward. A natural phrasing is “他不跟我住在一个小区.”

column2: His body is frail.
column4: “身体薄弱” is not the natural expression; say “身体虚弱.”

column2: He turned to a new direction.
column4: “Turned to a new direction” is unnatural; say “turned in a new direction.”

column2: He lives at ease.
column4: “He lives at ease” is unnatural English; “He lives comfortably” is more natural.

column2: He hasn't come already, has he?
column4: “Hasn't come already” is unnatural here; the natural wording is “He hasn't come yet, has he?”

column2: He is still sleeping.
column4: To say “is still sleeping,” use 他还在睡觉.

column2: He has nothing in him.
column4: “He has nothing in him” is not a natural way to say that he is good for nothing.

column1: 他这么说就是为了开玩笑。
column2: He said it merely as a joke.
column4: “为了开玩笑” is awkward; a native speaker would more naturally say “只是开玩笑” or “为了开个玩笑.”

column2: It's pitiful he does this.
column4: “It's pitiful he does this” is awkward English; “It's pitiful that he does this” is more natural.

column2: PH
column4: “PH”不是可理解的英文翻译。

column2: He fell into difficulty.
column4: 陷入困难 is an unnatural collocation; say 陷入困境 or 遇到困难.

column2: He was very patient.
column4: The Chinese says he is very patient, not that he was patient.

column2: He booked a doctor.
column4: “Booked a doctor” is unnatural; say “made an appointment with a doctor.”

column2: He took off to the south.
column4: 中文说他飞到了南方，英文“took off”只表示起飞。

column1: 付出什么，就会得到什么。
column2: What you give, you will get it back.
column4: 中文表达付出与回报相应，英文的“get it back”则表示把所给之物拿回来。

column2: What would you like to do in the future?
column4: “打算” means to plan or intend to do something, not simply to want to.

column1: 以咖啡来作一顿饭的结束。
column2: Coffee ends a meal.
column4: The Chinese is a sentence fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column2: If the price is right, I'll buy.
column4: “价合理” is ungrammatical here; use “价格合理” or “价钱合理.”

column2: It costs 25 dollars and 50 cents.
column4: The Chinese price is in yuan and mao, not dollars and cents.

column2: The meeting's theme is eco-protection.
column4: “Eco-protection” is not a natural English term here; say “environmental protection.”

column2: sadly cry
column4: Both sides are verb phrases, not complete sentences.

column2: I guess it's only a joke.
column4: “估计那就是个笑话吧” means “I guess that’s a joke”; “only” adds a meaning not present in the Chinese.

column2: I wish she had come last night.
column4: 但愿她昨晚来就好了不自然；可以说“要是她昨晚来了就好了”。

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not an English translation.

column2: live very comfortably
column4: Both sides are verb phrases, not complete sentences.

column2: Have you finishing doing homework?
column4: “Have you finishing” is ungrammatical; say “Have you finished doing your homework?”

column2: It only took you just one night to finish reading it?
column4: “Only took you just” is redundant and unnatural; say “Did it only take you one night to finish reading it?”

column2: You've been very good.
column4: “一向来” is an unnatural combination here.

column1: 你一定要考虑清楚你想做怎么样的工作。
column2: You must consider what kind of work you want to do.
column4: “怎么样的工作” is awkward here; “什么样的工作” is the natural phrasing.

column2: You might as well go kill yourself.
column4: This is an abusive, harmful statement.

column1: 你不希望我和你一起去吗？
column2: Don't you wish you were going with me?
column4: The Chinese asks whether you want me to go with you; the English asks whether I wish I were going with you.

column2: You shouldn't have done it.
column4: “你不应该做的” is a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column1: 你不必什么都非得自己来。
column2: You shouldn't try to do everything by yourself.
column4: “不必” means you don't have to; “shouldn't” expresses advice not to.

column2: You don't need to be there.
column4: “去那里” means to go there, while “be there” means to be there.

column1: 你不懂这句句子，不是吗？
column2: You can't understand this sentence, can you?
column4: “这句句子” is unnatural; say “这句话” or “这个句子.”

column2: You didn't need to explain.
column4: “你不用说明的” means you don’t need to explain, not that you didn’t need to explain.

column1: 你不能从早到晚不吃东西。
column2: You can't eat nothing from morning to night.
column4: “You can't eat nothing” is an awkward double negative; the intended meaning is “You can't go without eating anything.”

column2: You must not eat too much.
column4: 不该 means “shouldn’t”; “must not” is stronger.

column1: 你为什么会出现在我工作单位？
column2: Why would you appear in my unit?
column4: 工作单位 means “workplace,” not “unit.”

column1: 你为什么这么早来到了？
column2: Why did you come this early?
column4: “来到了”在这里不自然；通常说“你为什么这么早就来了？”

column2: When have you ever done anything for me?
column4: The Chinese asks when you do work for me; the English asks whether you have ever done anything for me.

column1: 你什么时候需要交作文？
column2: When have you got to hand in your essay?
column4: “When have you got to…” is awkward here; “When do you have to hand in your essay?” is natural.

column2: Are you watching TV today?
column4: The Chinese asks whether you have watched TV today, while the English asks whether you are watching it today.

column2: Would you mind closing the window?
column4: The Chinese asks whether the speaker may close the window; the English asks whether the listener will close it.

column2: You can see it from as far as over there.
column4: “你从那里就看得到了” is not a natural way to say this; use “你从那里就能看到了” or “你在那儿就看得到.”

column1: 你们会待在日本到什么时候？
column2: Until when will you stay in Japan?
column4: “Until when” is unnatural here; say “How long will you stay in Japan?”

column1: 你们做饭用天然气还是用电？
column2: Do you cook by gas or electricity?
column4: “Cook by gas or electricity” is unnatural; say “cook with gas or electricity.”

column1: 你们冷静下来，从头开始跟我说。
column2: Calm down, and listen to me speak from the beginning.
column4: “跟我说” means “tell me,” not “listen to me speak.”

column1: 你们应该收集进一步的信息。
column2: You must gather further information.
column4: “应该”是“should”，语气弱于英文的“must”。

column2: Do you have a table in the patio?
column4: A table is usually said to be “on the patio,” not “in the patio.”

column2: Were you guys serious?
column4: The Chinese asks if they are serious now; the English asks whether they were serious in the past.

column1: 你们晚上到哪儿吃饭啊？
column2: Where will you all go to eat food this evening?
column4: “Go to eat food” is unnatural here; say “Where will you all go for dinner tonight?”

column2: your food
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: Can you help out?
column4: The Chinese asks whether you can help us, but the English omits “us.”

column2: How many rental cars do you want?
column4: “出租车” means taxis, not rental cars.

column2: You people can't help yourselves.
column4: The Chinese says you people won't be able to get it done; it does not mean you can't help yourselves.

column1: 你们这里有可爱动物区吗？
column2: Do you have a petting zoo area?
column4: 可爱动物区 means a cute-animal area, not specifically a petting zoo.

column2: Do you ever rest?
column4: 你休息过吗 asks whether you've rested; “Do you ever rest?” asks about a habit.

column2: What would you do?
column4: “你会做什么？” usually asks what you can or will do, not what you would do hypothetically.

column2: Your future is bright.
column4: 你会前途无量的 is unnatural. Say 你前途无量 or 你的前途无量.

column1: 你会希望你从来没有看过它。
column2: You will wish you had never seen it.
column4: “你会希望你……” sounds unnatural here; a native speaker would more naturally say “你会希望自己从来没看过它。”

column2: Do you understand French?
column4: “会法语” means knowing or speaking French, not specifically understanding it.

column2: Jump as high as you can.
column4: The natural expression is “你能跳多高就跳多高”; “会” is not idiomatic here.

column2: Your son has come of age.
column4: “现在成人了”不自然；通常说“现在成年了”。

column2: How many accounts do you have?
column4: 这句话缺少“有”；自然的说法是“你有几个用户名呀？”

column1: 你刚才把一个玩意儿落在桌上了。
column2: You just put a toy down on the table.
column4: “玩意儿” means a thing, not specifically a toy, and “落在桌上” means it was left or ended up on the table, not that someone put it there.

column1: 你到底想不想谈那件事？
column2: Don't you want to talk about it at all?
column4: The Chinese asks whether the person wants to talk about it or not; the English instead asks whether they don’t want to talk about it at all.

column1: 你午饭吃的不多，不是吗？
column2: You didn't eat much lunch, did you?
column4: The aspect marker should be written “得”: 你午饭吃得不多，不是吗？

column1: 你去跑步的时候叫我一声。
column2: Give me a ring when you go running.
column4: “叫我一声” means to let me know or call out to me, not specifically to phone me.

column2: Did you go to the supermarket?
column4: 去过 asks whether someone has ever been to the supermarket; “Did you go” asks about a specific past trip.

column1: 你可以休息在草地上，但是别踩它。
column2: You can relax on the grass, but don't trample it.
column4: “休息在草地上” is unnatural; say “在草地上休息.”

column1: 你可以来一下我的办公室吗？
column2: Could you please come to my office?
column4: “来一下我的办公室” is unnatural; say “来我的办公室一下” or “来一下我办公室.”

column2: You may sit as you like.
column4: “随意坐”不自然地表达入座；通常说“请随便坐”或“你可以随便坐”。

column2: Come on any day you like.
column4: “随时”表示任何时间，英文却限定为“any day”。

column2: Eat noodles.
column4: The Chinese is phrased as a statement (“You eat noodles”), while the English is a command.

column1: 你告诉她你已经在三天前完成这个工作了。
column2: You told her that you had finished the work three days before.
column4: “已经在三天前完成” is unnatural; say “三天前已经完成”.

column2: you and I
column4: This is a phrase, not a complete sentence.

column1: 你和我其中一个要出席这次的会议。
column2: Either you or I must attend the meeting.
column4: “你和我其中一个” is awkward; a natural phrasing is “我们俩中有一个要出席这次会议。”

column2: Do you like to be alone?
column4: 一个人 can mean “someone”; the Chinese doesn't clearly mean “to be alone.”

column1: 你喜欢哪一种法国红酒？
column2: What's your favorite French wine?
column4: The Chinese asks which kind of French red wine you like, not what your favorite French wine is.

column2: Have you drank tea?
column4: “Have you drank” is ungrammatical; it should be “Have you drunk tea?”

column2: How did you reply?
column4: 你回答了什么？ asks what you answered, not how you replied.

column1: 你在你的车上装雪地轮了吗？
column2: Have you put winter tyres on your car yet?
column4: “雪地轮”不是自然的轮胎说法，通常说“雪地胎”或“雪胎”。

column2: You are behind the mountain!
column4: “你在后山” means you are on/at the back hill, not behind the mountain.

column2: What are you doing home?
column4: “What are you doing home?” is ungrammatical; say “What are you doing at home?”

column2: You are at work.
column4: “你在工作” means “You are working,” not necessarily “You are at work.”

column2: What're you reading?
column4: 看什么 means “What are you looking at?” or “What are you watching?”; “reading” is not specified.

column2: How often do you have to see the dentist?
column4: The English adds that seeing the dentist is required (“have to”), which the Chinese does not say.

column2: How heavy you are!
column4: 你多重啊！ asks how much someone weighs, while “How heavy you are!” is an exclamation.

column2: How's your daughter?
column4: “你女儿怎么了？” asks what is wrong with your daughter, rather than asking generally how she is.

column2: Hello, girl with the red dress!
column4: 红衣服 means red clothes, not specifically a red dress.

column2: You are not at all wrong.
column4: “You are not at all wrong” is awkward English; a natural translation is “You’re absolutely right.”

column1: 你家桌子边有几个椅子？
column2: How many chairs do you have around your table?
column4: “椅子”通常用量词“把”；应说“几个把椅子”或更自然地说“几把椅子”。

column2: How far is your house away from here?
column4: “How far is your house away from here?” is unnatural English. Say “How far is your house from here?”

column1: 你家里的女生都比你大吗？
column2: Are your sisters all older than you?
column4: “你家里的女生” is not a natural way to refer to the women or sisters in your family.

column2: What's your impression of that person like?
column4: “What's your impression of that person like?” is ungrammatical. A natural version is “What's your impression of that person?”

column2: You are going to drive me crazy!
column4: “将要……了” is awkward here; a natural phrasing is “你要把我逼疯了！”

column2: You've had plenty of chances to do that.
column4: The English adds “to do that,” specifying what the chances were for, but the Chinese does not.

column1: 你应该先从最简单的问题开始。
column2: You should begin with easier questions.
column4: “最简单的问题” means “the easiest questions,” not merely “easier questions.”

column2: You should do the honorable thing and resign.
column4: “光荣地辞职” sounds unnatural in this context; it does not naturally express doing the honorable thing by resigning.

column2: You should have visited Kyoto.
column4: The final 的 is unnatural here; say “你应该参观京都.”

column2: You should've woken me.
column4: “你应该叫醒我”表示现在或将来应该叫醒我；“You should’ve woken me”表示过去本该叫醒我。

column1: 你应该好好利用这个机会。
column2: You had better make use of the opportunity.
column4: “应该” means “should”; “had better” is stronger advice.

column2: You deserve the prize.
column4: “奖金” means a monetary bonus or prize money, not simply “the prize.”

column1: 你应该理解，这是严肃的。
column2: You should understand, this is serious.
column4: “这是严肃的” is unnatural here; say “这是很严肃的事.”

column1: 你应该给他看看这装置。
column2: You should have shown him the device.
column4: “你应该给他看看” means you should show him, not that you should have shown him.

column1: 你应该要更快警告他的。
column2: You should have warned him sooner.
column4: “更快” means more quickly, not sooner or earlier.

column1: 你弟弟要在我们家住到什么时候？
column2: Your younger brother is going to stay in our house until when?
column4: “Until when” is unnatural here; say “until what time” or “how long.”

column2: Who do you think you are?
column4: “你当你是谁啊” is not a natural way to say this; use “你以为你是谁啊？”

column2: How are you always unhappy?
column4: “你怎么……” asks why, but “How are you always unhappy?” asks how.

column2: Why are you so anxious!
column4: “你怎么这么要紧” is not a natural way to say someone is anxious.

column2: What kind of dessert would you like?
column4: “你想什么甜点” is not a natural way to ask what dessert someone would like; “你想要什么甜点？” would be natural.

column2: Where would you like to go watch?
column4: 看看 means to have a look or look around, not “watch.”

column2: Would you like to go travel?
column4: “Would you like to go travel?” is ungrammatical; say “Would you like to travel?” or “Would you like to go traveling?”

column2: How do you want your hair cut?
column4: “你想将头发剪成怎样” is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “你想把头发剪成什么样？”

column2: Can you think of any examples?
column4: 想得到例子 is not a natural way to ask whether someone can think of examples; 你能想到例子吗 would be natural.

column2: Would you like to play video games?
column4: 中文问的是是否想要电玩；英文问的是是否想玩电子游戏。

column2: Follow your desire.
column4: The Chinese says what you want is the most important; the English says to follow your desire.

column2: Who do you think came to see me yesterday?
column4: “你才昨天谁来找我了？” is ungrammatical; the words do not form a natural question.

column2: Did you call me on the phone?
column4: The Chinese asks whether you call me, not whether you called me in the past.

column2: Do you offer any all-day tours?
column4: “全日游” is not the usual natural phrasing here; “一日游” is more idiomatic.

column1: 你收到了我发的邮件了吗？
column2: Did you get my letter?
column4: 邮件 means email, not letter.

column2: the students that you teach / taught
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.

column1: 你明天下午有什么安排？
column2: Any plan for tomorrow afternoon?
column4: “Any plan” is unnatural here; say “Any plans for tomorrow afternoon?”

column1: 你明天这个时候会是在做什么？
column2: What'll you be doing at this time tomorrow?
column4: “会是” makes the sentence awkward; say “你明天这个时候会在做什么？”

column1: 你最会操作这台机器了。
column2: You understand best how to use the machine.
column4: The Chinese says you are best at operating the machine; the English says you understand best how to use it.

column2: What was the worst day of your life?
column4: The Chinese asks how the worst day was; it does not say “of your life” or clearly ask what that day was.

column1: 你最好不要开了我的车。
column2: You'd better not have driven my car.
column4: “不要开了我的车” is ungrammatical in this context. Say “你最好不要开我的车” for “You’d better not drive my car.”

column1: 你最近有听到什么不寻常的事吗？
column2: Did you hear anything unusual lately?
column4: “Did you hear ... lately?”不自然；通常说“Have you heard anything unusual lately?”

column2: Can you run as fast as Bolt does?
column4: “你有Bolt跑得快吗” is not a natural way to ask whether someone runs as fast as Bolt. Say “你跑得有Bolt快吗？”

column2: Do you have something?
column4: “Do you have something?” is unnatural in this context; “Is something the matter?” or “Do you need something?” is more natural.

column2: Whatever words you have, just say them.
column4: “Whatever words you have” is unnatural in English; the sentence means “Whatever you want to say, just say it.”

column2: What's your problem?
column4: “What's your problem?” is confrontational, while the Chinese can simply ask what question or issue someone has.

column1: 你有听到他说得有多快吗？
column2: Did you hear how quickly he speaks?
column4: The Chinese asks how fast he spoke, while “he speaks” describes the present or a habitual action.

column2: Were you able to do it?
column4: The Chinese asks about ability now; the English asks whether you were able to do it in the past.

column2: Has your friend divorced?
column4: “Has your friend divorced?” is unnatural; say “Has your friend gotten divorced?”

column1: 你永远没有第二次机会去打造第一印象。
column2: You never get a second chance to make a first impression.
column4: “打造第一印象” is not a natural expression here; “留下第一印象” is more idiomatic.

column2: You haven't been listening.
column4: “你没听” means “You didn’t listen”; it doesn’t express the ongoing sense of “haven’t been listening.”

column2: Don't you have a phone number?
column4: “电话”指电话或手机，不是“phone number”。

column2: When did your father come home?
column4: “什么时候回家” asks when he comes or will come home, not when he came home.

column1: 你的头发和我的头发一样长。
column2: You hair is as long as mine.
column4: “You hair” should be “Your hair.”

column1: 你的头发自然发色是什么颜色？
column2: What's your natural hair color?
column4: “头发自然发色” is awkward; a native speaker would more naturally say “你的自然发色是什么颜色？”

column2: Where did your sister just go?
column4: “你的妹妹呢？” means “What about your younger sister?” or “Where is your younger sister?” It does not say she just went somewhere.

column1: 你的姐姐游泳得不好，是不是？
column2: Your sister can't swim well, can she?
column4: “游泳得不好” is not natural here; say “游泳游得不好” or “游得不好.”

column2: What are your influences?
column4: “影响力”指影响他人的能力；英文“your influences”指对你产生影响的人或事。

column2: your cell phone
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: How much was your cell phone?
column4: The Chinese asks how much the phone costs; the English asks how much it cost in the past.

column2: Is your watch correct?
column4: “Is your watch correct?” is not a natural way to ask whether a watch keeps accurate time.

column1: 你的演说十分精彩，但竟没人懂得欣赏。
column2: Your wonderful lecture was pearls before swine.
column4: “Pearls before swine” implies the audience is unworthy; the Chinese only says nobody appreciates the lecture.

column2: Where is your phone?
column4: “你的电话是哪里的？”通常是在问电话或号码来自哪里，不是问手机在哪里。

column1: 你的眼睛不要看著地上;看著我。
column2: Don't keep your eyes on the ground; look at me.
column4: “眼睛不要看着地上”不自然；更自然的说法是“别看着地上”或“别盯着地上看”。

column2: Your manners aren't very good.
column4: “你的礼貌不是很好” sounds unnatural; a native speaker would more likely say “你不太有礼貌。”

column2: Your dress is very nice.
column4: 穿著 refers to someone’s attire or outfit generally, not specifically a dress.

column2: Your speech sucked.
column4: “讲词” is not a natural way to say “speech” here; use “演讲” or “讲话”.

column2: What you see is what you get.
column4: The Chinese means “Take whatever you see,” not “What you see is what you get.”

column1: 你看完这本书要多少时间？
column2: How long did it take you to finish reading that book?
column4: The Chinese asks how long it takes or will take, while the English asks how long it took in the past.

column1: 你看起来像一个聪明人。
column2: You seem like a very smart person.
column4: The English adds “very”; the Chinese only says he seems like a smart person.

column2: You look pretty ill.
column4: 气色不太好 means someone doesn’t look well or has a poor complexion; “pretty ill” says they look quite sick.

column1: 你真的要试着那样做吗？
column2: Is it true you're trying to do that?
column4: The Chinese asks whether the person is really going to try doing it; the English asks whether they are currently trying.

column1: 你知道公园街上往前有家中餐馆吗？
column2: Did you know there used to be a Chinese restaurant on Park Street?
column4: The Chinese asks whether there is a restaurant there; the English says there used to be one.

column1: 你知道商场什么时候关门吗？
column2: Do you know when the supermarket closes?
column4: “商场” means “shopping mall,” not “supermarket.”

column2: Do you know how to speak?
column4: 怎么说 means “how to say [it],” not “how to speak.”

column1: 你知道怎样到我们这儿吗？
column2: Do you know how to get to us here?
column4: “Get to us here” is awkward; “get here to where we are” or “get to our place” would be more natural.

column1: 你确知你还从未遇见过她？
column2: You're certain that you've never met her before?
column4: “确知” sounds unnatural here; a native speaker would more naturally say “你确定你以前从没见过她？”

column1: 你竟然做出那样的事来，你还是人吗？
column2: It is wicked of you to do such things.
column4: The Chinese also asks “Are you even human?”—a significant accusation omitted from the English.

column2: Are you married or are you single?
column4: For an either-or question, Chinese normally uses 还是, not 或: 你结婚了还是没结婚？

column1: 你给他们的钱会用到好处。
column2: The money you give them will be put to good use.
column4: “钱会用到好处” is not a natural Chinese expression. A natural phrasing is “这笔钱会得到善用”.

column2: You sing songs to me.
column4: 你给我唱歌 is naturally read as a request or command, while “You sing songs to me” is a statement.

column2: You must be mentally exhausted.
column4: “脑子糊掉了” suggests that someone’s thinking is muddled, not that they are mentally exhausted.

column1: 你能再向我解释一遍你为什么迟到了吗？
column2: Could you please tell me again why you are late?
column4: The Chinese refers to why you were late, while the English asks why you are late.

column2: Can you finish eating all?
column4: “Can you finish eating all?” is unnatural; say “Can you finish eating it all?”

column2: Can you answer this question?
column4: “问题”通常用量词“个”，不是“条”；说“你能回答这个问题吗？”

column1: 你能来的话我会很开心。
column2: I'd be delighted if you could come with us.
column4: The English adds “with us,” which is not stated in the Chinese.

column2: You could run.
column4: “你能跑” means “You can run”; “could” suggests past ability or a more tentative possibility.

column2: How long did it take you to learn Japanese?
