column4: The Chinese asks how long you spend learning Japanese, while the English asks how long it took you.

column2: Do you want wine?
column4: “酒” means alcoholic drink or liquor in general; it does not specifically mean wine.

column1: 你觉得别人都是傻子吗？就你聪明？
column2: Do you think everyone else is an idiot? That only you are smart?
column4: “That only you are smart?” is not a natural or grammatical English question.

column2: Do you think there's a hope?
column4: “There's a hope” is unnatural here; say “Is there any hope?”

column2: Who do you think made the mistake?
column4: “谁是错误的” asks who is wrong, not who made a mistake.

column2: Do you know John?
column4: “胡安” is Juan, not John.

column2: You must study more.
column4: “你该” means “you should/ought to,” not the stronger “you must.”

column2: You should've stayed in the car.
column4: 你该留在车里 means “You should stay in the car,” not “You should’ve stayed.”

column2: You should come over.
column4: “你该过来的” means “You should have come over,” not “You should come over.”

column2: You and me are the same age.
column4: “You and me” is ungrammatical as the subject; use “You and I.”

column2: Who were you talking to?
column4: The Chinese asks who you are talking to now; the English asks who you were talking to.

column1: 你身体一直非常好，怎么突然间住医院了？
column2: Your body was always very healthy; why are you suddenly in the hospital?
column4: “住医院”不自然；通常说“住院”。

column2: Aren't you looking for work?
column4: “还在” means “still”; the English negative question changes the meaning.

column2: You're still green.
column4: “You're still green”通常指缺乏经验，不是“你还年轻”。

column1: 你还知道花闻起来是怎样的吗？
column2: Do you even know how to smell the flowers?
column4: The Chinese asks whether you know what flowers smell like; the English asks whether you know how to smell them.

column1: 你这样做是害他，而不是帮他。
column2: By doing this you were hurting him, not helping him.
column4: The Chinese describes the action generally or in the present, while “you were hurting him” places it in the past.

column2: You are a disappointing person!
column4: The Chinese asks whether people like you are lousy, while the English states that you are disappointing.

column2: Are you troubled?
column4: “Are you troubled?” is not a natural translation here; say “Are you in trouble?”.

column2: Leave the room as it is.
column4: “保留原状地离开房间” is not a natural way to say this in Chinese.

column1: 假如有一点机会，我就会辞去现在的工作。
column2: If I just had some other opportunity, I would quit my job.
column4: “Some other opportunity” adds the idea of another opportunity; the Chinese just says there is a chance/opportunity.

column2: Have a good dream!
column4: “Have a good dream!” is not a natural English expression; “Sweet dreams!” is idiomatic.

column2: One should be courteous.
column4: “做人要讲礼” is not a natural phrasing; “做人要讲礼貌” or “做人要懂礼数” is more idiomatic.

column1: 做出这个结论花了我们三个小时。
column2: We spent three hours to come to this conclusion.
column4: “We spent three hours to come to this conclusion” is not idiomatic; say “We spent three hours coming to this conclusion.”

column2: do very well
column4: This is a verb phrase, not a sentence.

column2: Dream.
column4: “做梦吧” commonly means “Dream on,” not simply “Dream.”

column2: Business is for profit.
column4: “为了利”不自然；通常说“为了赚钱”或“为了利益”。

column2: Business needs credit.
column4: 讲信用 means keeping one’s word or being trustworthy, not needing credit.

column2: Business needs good faith.
column4: “Business needs good faith” is unnatural here; “Doing business requires integrity” is more idiomatic.

column2: Business must follow the legal system.
column4: “遵守法制” is unnatural here; one would normally say “遵守法律.”

column2: Those who forget everything are happy.
column4: “健忘的人” means forgetful people, not people who forget everything.

column2: Stealing is evil.
column4: “偷东西是罪恶” sounds unnatural here; “偷东西是犯罪” or “偷东西是不对的” is more idiomatic.

column2: Capricious as April.
column4: 这是一个短语，不是完整句子。

column1: 像那样的老师还是别干了比较好。
column2: Such a teacher may as well retire from his work.
column4: “别干了” means they should stop doing the job, not specifically retire.

column1: 儿童和成人的票价不同。
column2: Tickets differ for children and adults.
column4: The Chinese says the ticket prices differ for children and adults; the English says the tickets themselves differ.

column2: Rabbits and monkeys are cute.
column4: “兔”和“猴” sound unnatural as standalone animal names here; say “兔子和猴子.”

column1: 入住前要付押金。还有，不能带宠物。
column2: You need to pay the deposit before using the room. Also, you're not allowed to have pets here.
column4: “入住前” means before checking in, not before using the room.

column2: Admission to the show is $5.
column4: 入场费是五元，通常指五元人民币；the English says $5.

column2: A nationwide unified exam.
column4: Both sides are noun phrases rather than complete sentences.
This is a time expression, not a sentence.

column2: It's business.
column4: “公事公办” means handling official or work matters impartially, not simply “It’s business.”

column2: The bus stop isn't far from us.
column4: The location phrase is unnatural; say “公交车站离我们很近。”

column1: 公元两千年以后，北京举办过运动会。
column2: Beijing hosted the games in 2008 AD.
column4: The Chinese only says Beijing hosted a sporting event sometime after 2000; it does not specify 2008.

column1: 公司在搞促销，很多商品优惠。
column2: The firm has promotions with discounts.
column4: “很多商品优惠” is unnatural; say “很多商品有优惠” or “很多商品在打折.”

column2: The company innovates technology.
column4: “Innovates technology” is unnatural English; say “is innovating its technology” or “is developing new technology.”

column2: The company opens to outside.

column4: “placeholder-p11”不是英文句子。

column2: In about two weeks.
column4: Both are context-dependent fragments rather than complete sentences.

column2: Life in big cities is fast.
column4: “生活很快” is not a natural way to describe the pace of city life. Say “大都市的生活节奏很快”.

column2: It's cold; he draped on a coat.
column4: “Draped on a coat” is not idiomatic; say “put on a coat.”

column2: It's getting warmer day by day.
column4: “天日渐回暖” is unnatural; say “天气日渐回暖.”

column2: The weather warmed.
column4: “The weather warmed” is unnatural in this context; say “The weather got warmer.”

column2: The sun is setting.
column4: “太阳下山了” means the sun has set, not that it is setting.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not an English translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: Cows give milk, made into powder.
column4: “Cows give milk, made into powder” is grammatically awkward; the second clause needs a clear subject.

column1: 她一口气喝下半杯多凉茶。
column2: She gulped down half her tea in one mouthful.
column4: 半杯多 means more than half a cup, not simply half her tea.

column2: She woke up in the early morning.
column4: “起床”是从床上起来，英文“woke up”是醒来。

column2: She didn't have any pencils.
column4: The Chinese states present possession, while the English says she did not have pencils in the past.

column2: She came here as soon as she heard it.
column4: The Chinese says she heard it as soon as she arrived; the English says she arrived as soon as she heard it.

column2: She disliked him.
column4: The Chinese says she does not like him, while the English puts it in the past.

column2: She disliked her husband.
column4: The Chinese says she doesn't like her husband, while the English says she disliked him.

column2: I was lonely without her.
column4: The Chinese describes feeling lonely now, while the English puts it in the past.

column2: She was in no humor for lunch.
column4: “In no humor for lunch” is not a natural English expression; “in no mood for lunch” would be natural.

column2: She wasn't able to meet him.
column4: The Chinese says she cannot meet him, while the English says she was unable to meet him in the past.

column2: Her eyes are dark.
column4: “她两眼于墨黑” is ungrammatical Chinese.

column2: She did everything for her.
column4: “做了一切事” sounds unnatural; say “为她做了一切” or “为她做了所有的事”.

column2: She made the doll for me.
column4: 中文说的是“这个娃娃”（this doll），英文说的是“the doll”。

column2: When was she born?
column4: 她什么时候生的？通常 asks when she gave birth, not when she was born.

column1: 她什么都放辣，连汤都是辣的。
column2: She put spice in everything. Even the soup is spicy.
column4: “放辣” is not a natural way to say “add something spicy”; say “放辣椒” or “放辣的东西.”

column2: She studies 24 / 7.
column4: “24/7” means around the clock, while the Chinese says she studies from morning to night.

column2: They are both good students.
column4: “Both” specifies two students, while “她们都是” means all of them and does not specify how many.

column2: She lives in Madrid.
column4: “住” needs 在 before the place here: “她住在马德里”.

column2: He advised me not to believe what she says.
column4: The Chinese uses 她 (“she”), but the English says “He.”

column2: She sang better than him.
column4: The Chinese says she sings better than him, not that she sang better.

column1: 她回答说她从来没有见过那个男人。
column2: Her answer was that she never had seen that man.
column4: The natural word order is “she had never seen that man.”

column2: She got off at the next station.
column4: “下一个站”不自然；通常说“下一站”。

column1: 她在二十岁的时候生下第一个孩子。
column2: She gave birth to her first child at twenty years old.
column4: “At twenty years old” is awkward; say “at age twenty” or “when she was twenty.”

column2: She has a house by the sea.
column4: “有所房子” is not natural; say “有一所房子” or “有房子”.

column1: 她在等的那个男孩是我的一个朋友。
column2: The girl waiting for that boy is a friend of mine.
column4: The Chinese says she is waiting for a boy; the English says a girl is waiting for that boy.

column2: She is a clerk in the supermarket.
column4: 秘书 means “secretary,” not “clerk.”

column2: His big sister has never travelled to China.
column4: The Chinese says her older sister didn’t go on a trip to China; the English says his sister has never traveled to China.

column1: 她对她的孩子非常生气。
column2: She got very angry with her children.
column4: 对她的孩子非常生气 describes being very angry, not necessarily becoming angry.

column1: 她屏着气息，躲了在门的后面。
column2: She hid behind the door and held her breath.
column4: “躲了在门的后面” is ungrammatical; say “躲在门后面.”

column2: She's already sleeping.
column4: 她已经睡下了 means she has already gone to bed, not necessarily that she is already sleeping.

column2: She would often play tricks on me.
column4: 开我的玩笑 means “make fun of me” or “tease me,” not “play tricks on me.”

column2: She extended her stay by five days.
column4: “延长停留五天” is awkward; a more natural phrasing is “把停留时间延长了五天”.

column2: Is she a taxi driver?
column4: The Chinese asks whether she drives a taxi; the English asks whether she is a taxi driver.

column2: She is kind.
column4: “她很好” means she is good or well; it does not specifically mean she is kind.

column1: 她很怕和她父母讲这件事。
column2: She was afraid to tell her parents.
column4: The Chinese describes her fear in the present or generally; the English says she was afraid in the past.

column1: 她很适合做像市场推广之类的工作。
column2: She's very suitable for jobs like marketing and similar.
column4: “Jobs like marketing and similar” is unnatural; say “jobs like marketing and the like.”

column2: The girl has a sweet heart.
column4: “The girl” adds a specific age/description not present in “她,” and “has a sweet heart” is an unnatural way to express that she is kind-hearted.

column2: She was busy with housework.
column4: The Chinese describes her as busy with housework now; the English puts it in the past.

column2: She was in a hurry to see her father.
column4: “急于见” means eager to see, not necessarily in a hurry to see.

column2: She wanted to go over a few things with him.
column4: “想” is present-oriented, while “wanted” places the desire in the past.

column2: She wanted to be famous.
column4: 她想出名 expresses a present desire; “wanted” puts it in the past.

column2: She wants to drink some warm milk.
column4: “一点温奶” sounds unnatural; “一点温牛奶” is more idiomatic.

column2: She wants a new hat.
column4: “顶” needs a numeral here: “她想要一顶新帽子。”

column1: 她把大部分钱都用在买裙子上了。
column2: She spends most of her money on her dresses.
column4: The Chinese describes a completed past action, while the English says she spends the money in the present.

column1: 她把头从窗户外缩回来。
column2: She withdrew her head from a window.
column4: “从窗户外缩回来” is an unnatural way to say she pulled her head back from the window.

column2: She has anxiety for your safety.
column4: “Has anxiety for your safety” is unnatural English; say “She is worried about your safety.”

column2: She drew up the curtain.
column4: “拉上窗帘” means she pulled the curtain closed, not that she drew it up.

column1: 她挥着她的手，直到火车消失在视线之外。
column2: She waved her hand until the train was out of sight.
column4: 挥着她的手 is unnatural here; a native speaker would normally say 她挥手.

column1: 她接下来说你应该遵守你的承诺。
column2: She continued that you should keep your promise.
column4: “Continued that” is ungrammatical here; say “continued by saying that” or “went on to say that.”

column1: 她提出了一连串的医学发现。
column2: She made a series of medical discoveries.
column4: 提出了一连串的医学发现 is an unnatural collocation; discoveries are usually described as being made.

column1: 她摸黑摸不到灯的开关。
column2: She groped for the light switch in the dark.
column4: The Chinese says she couldn’t find the light switch in the dark; the English only says she groped for it.

column1: 她是一个奇怪，神秘和鼓舞人心的诗人。
column2: She's a strange, enigmatic and inspiring poet.
column4: The list sounds unnatural; a native speaker would more likely say “一个奇怪、神秘又鼓舞人心的诗人”.

column2: She's a blog addict.
column4: 微博 refers specifically to Weibo, not blogs in general.

column1: 她是我认识的最烦人的女孩。
column2: She is the most boring girl I ever knew.
column4: “烦人的” means annoying, not boring.

column2: She is a young artist.
column4: “文艺青年” describes a young person with artistic or literary interests, not necessarily a young artist.

column2: She is angry, and still tired.
column4: The Chinese asks whether she is angry or tired; the English says she is angry and still tired.

column1: 她曾是班上唱歌绝对的第一名。
column2: She was by far the best singer in the class.
column4: “唱歌绝对的第一名” is unnatural phrasing. A natural version is “她曾是班上唱歌唱得最好的。”

column1: 她最讨厌抽烟的男人了。
column2: She most hates men that smoke.
column4: “She most hates” is unnatural English; say “She hates men who smoke the most.”

column2: She has put on weight recently.
column4: “增加了体重” is unnatural here; a native speaker would say “体重增加了” or “长胖了”.

column2: She has an eye for beauty.
column4: 她有一双美丽的眼睛 means she has beautiful eyes, not that she has an eye for beauty.

column1: 她有很多缺点，但我还是这么信她。
column2: She has many faults, but I trust her none the less.
column4: “我还是这么信她” means “I still trust her this much/like this,” not simply “I trust her nonetheless.”

column2: She was ill with heart disease.
column4: The Chinese says she has heart disease; the English changes it to a past illness.

column1: 她有时会一动不动的坐上好几个小时。
column2: She will sometimes sit still for hours.
column4: “坐”作状语应写“地坐”，不是“的坐”。

column1: 她毫无间断地照顾自己的孩子。
column2: She always takes care of her children.
column4: 毫无间断地 means “without interruption,” which is not conveyed by “always.”

column2: She didn't mean to disappoint him.
column4: “打击他” means to discourage or deal him a blow, not necessarily to disappoint him.

column1: 她没看到你的话就没有什么担心的。
column2: If she didn't see you then there’s nothing to worry about.
column4: “没看到你的话”不自然地表达“没看到你”；可说“如果她没看到你，就没什么可担心的”。

column2: She wept reading the letter.
column4: “她流泪看着信” is unnatural; say “她流着泪看信”.

column1: 她爸爸不会来的，他很忙。
column2: Her father won't come, he is really busy.
column4: The English joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

column1: 她理所当然的取得了胜利。
column2: She's sure to succeed.
column4: “理所当然地” requires “地,” not “的.”

column2: She wants cantaloupe for dessert.
column4: The word order is unnatural. Say “她想吃哈密瓜当甜点。”

column2: Her brother studies hard.
column4: 很认真学习 is unnatural; say 学习很认真 or 很认真地学习.

column1: 她的每首歌都长期备受欢迎。
column2: Every one of her songs was a hit.
column4: “长期备受欢迎” means the songs have remained popular for a long time, not simply that they were hits.

column2: She's on the rag.
column4: The Chinese says her old friend came; the English is an offensive idiom meaning she is menstruating.

column1: 她给男朋友打电话打到手机没电。
column2: She called her boyfriend and they kept talking until her phone was out of battery.
column4: “Out of battery” is unnatural English; say “her phone ran out of battery” or “her phone died.”

column2: She has the large house to herself.
column4: The Chinese says she gives herself a large house, not that she has a house to herself.

column2: She weeded the garden.
column4: She weeded the garden is usually 花园里除草 or 给花园除草; 她给花园除了草 is awkward.

column2: She went there by herself.
column4: “来那儿” means come there, while “went there” means go there.

column1: 她虽然可爱，但是我不喜欢她。
column2: She may be cute, but I don't like her.
column4: The Chinese states that she is cute; “may be cute” makes that uncertain.

column2: She had the boys paint the house.
column4: The Chinese says she wants the boys to paint the house; the English says she had them do it.

column1: 她让出个空间给一位老太太。
column2: She made room for an old lady.
column4: “让出个空间给” is unnatural here; a native speaker would more naturally say “给一位老太太腾出空间”.

column2: She had an individual style of speaking.
column4: The Chinese describes her speaking style in the present; the English says she had that style in the past.

column1: 她请了前台的人为她打那个号码。
column2: She has asked the person at the front desk to connect her to that number.
column4: The Chinese says she asked the person to dial the number; the English says to connect her to it.

column2: She dances folk dance.
column4: “She dances folk dance”表达不自然；可说“She does folk dancing”。

column2: She performs dance.
column4: “跳舞蹈” is not idiomatic; say “她跳舞”.

column2: She scraped her shoes clean before she entered the house.
column4: 擦鞋 means to wipe or polish shoes, not scrape them clean.

column1: 她连试图帮助他也没有。
column2: She didn't even attempt to help him.
column4: “她连试图帮助他也没有” is unnatural; “她甚至没有试图帮助他” is natural.

column2: She was absorbed in the video.
column4: “迷上了视频” means she got hooked on videos; it does not say she was absorbed in one video.

column1: 她需要一些钱来买点东西喂她的狗。
column2: She needed some money to buy something to feed her dog.
column4: The Chinese says she needs money, but the English says she needed it.

column2: She was very old.
column4: The Chinese says she is very old, while the English says she was very old.

column1: 她，这么说好了，是个活字典。
column2: She is, so to speak, a walking dictionary.
column4: “这么说好了” sounds unnatural as a parenthetical here; “这么说吧” would be more idiomatic.

column2: She seemed to have been ill.
column4: 好像她病了 means “It seems she’s ill” or “She seems to have gotten sick,” not that she seemed to have been ill in the past.

column2: I miss you so much.
column4: “好想见到你” means “I really want to see you,” not “I miss you so much.”

column2: Seems like we do know each other.
column4: 好象是认识 is an incomplete phrase without context; the English supplies “we” and “each other.”

column2: As you already know.
column4: This is a dependent phrase rather than a complete sentence, and needs a following clause.

column1: 如果不是太贵的话，我会买的。
column2: If it's not too expensive, I'll do that.
column4: “我会买的” means “I’ll buy it,” not the more general “I’ll do that.”

column1: 如果不是它很重要，我不会问你。
column2: I wouldn't ask this of you if it weren't important.
column4: “如果不是它很重要” is unnatural here; say “如果它不是很重要” or “如果不是因为它很重要”.

column1: 如果仍然有人缺席的，请将名单发给我。
column2: If anybody is still absent, please send their names to me.
column4: “如果仍然有人缺席的”不自然；应说“如果仍然有人缺席”。

column1: 如果你不想的话也没问题。
column2: If you don't want to do it, you don't have to.
column4: The Chinese says it is okay if you don’t want to; the English instead says you are not obliged to do it.

column2: If you can sing, that's good enough.
column4: “如果你会唱歌就好了” means “If only you could sing” or “It would be nice if you could sing,” not “If you can sing, that's good enough.”

column1: 如果你想学习好一种语言，自己学习它。
column2: If you want to learn a language well, learn it yourself.
column4: “学习好一种语言，自己学习它” is unnatural; a native speaker would more likely say “学好一门语言，自己学。”

column1: 如果地球停止自传，你认为会发生什么？
column2: What do you think would happen if the earth stopped spinning?
column4: “自传” means autobiography; the correct term for the Earth’s rotation is “自转”.

column1: 如果我了解这件事,我就会告诉你。
column2: If I could understand it, I would tell you so.
column4: “了解这件事” means knowing about the matter; “could understand it” changes that to being able to comprehend it.

column1: 如果没有你，我的人生就会变得空白一片。
column2: Life would become bland without you.
column4: “空白一片” means completely blank or empty, not bland.

column1: 如水流过鸭背般毫无反应。
column2: Like water off a duck's back.
column4: This is a fragment, not a complete sentence.

column2: Women plant flowers in the yard.
column4: “家园”通常不指住宅的院子；“院子” would be natural here.

column2: Women have the right to choose.
column4: “权力” means power or authority; “权利” would mean a right. The Chinese says women have the power to choose.

column1: 妈妈每个月都给我几百块钱。
column2: Mom gives me a couple hundred dollars every month.
column4: “块钱” means money/yuan, not specifically dollars.

column1: 妈妈看电视看了一晚上了。
column2: Mom has been watching TV all evening.
column4: “一晚上” means all night, while “all evening” is a shorter time span.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column1: 孙子和孙女照顾着爷爷。
column2: The grandchildren keep grandpa company.
column4: “照顾着” means they are taking care of Grandpa, not just keeping him company.

column1: 学外语要花好几年的时间才能学得精通。
column2: It takes years to master a foreign language.
column4: “学得精通” is unnatural; say “学到精通” or “学好”.“

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: The school is far, I go by bus.
column4: The English joins two independent clauses with a comma; use a period or a conjunction.

column1: 学校需要一个新的老师。
column2: The school needed a new teacher.
column4: 需要 means “needs,” not “needed.”

column2: In front of the school is a highway.
column4: “学校面前”不自然地表示学校前方；通常说“学校前面是一条公路”或“学校前面有一条公路”。

column2: You should not spoil a kid too much.
column4: “孩子不能太惯了”表达不自然；通常说“不能太惯孩子”或“孩子不能太娇惯”。

column1: 孩子们总爱创作自己的游戏。
column2: Children were apt to invent their own games.
column4: “总爱” describes a present habitual tendency, while “were apt to” describes a past tendency.

column1: 孩子们的衣食住行靠的是他们的父母。
column2: Children depend on their parents for food, clothing and shelter.
column4: 衣食住行 includes transportation, which is omitted from the English.

column2: The child sees pediatrics.
column4: “Sees pediatrics” is unnatural; say the child is being treated in the pediatrics department.

column2: The child plays a game console.
column4: “Plays a game console” is unnatural; say “plays games on a game console.”

column2: Children sometimes lack patience.
column4: “通常” means “usually,” not “sometimes.”

column1: 孩子长大了，应该照顾自己。
column2: The child has grown up and should take care of himself.
column4: “自己” does not specify gender, but “himself” does.

column2: Where does it leave from?
column4: “离开的” asks where it left from, while the English asks where it leaves from.

column2: I don't want either of them.
column4: The Chinese says none of them is what I want; the English says I want neither of them.

column2: It caught me by surprise.
column4: “它让我吓到” is not natural Mandarin; say “它吓到我了” or “它把我吓到了”.

column2: Crap, I didn't do the homework!
column4: 还没做 means the homework has not been done yet; “I didn't do” does not convey that it remains undone.

column2: Actually, it was pretty boring.
column4: “我非常无聊” means “I am very bored,” not “it was pretty boring.”

column2: the questions that the client asks / asked
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.

column1: 家里什么都没有，干脆出去吃吧。
column2: There is nothing in the house, let's just go out to eat.
column4: The English joins two independent clauses with a comma; use a period or semicolon instead.

column1: 对不起，我忘了作业这回事了。
column2: I'm sorry, I forgot to do my homework.
column4: 我忘了作业这回事了 means “I forgot about the homework,” not necessarily “I forgot to do my homework.”

column2: As for me, I have no objection.
column4: “对于我，我不反对” is unnatural; “对我来说，我不反对” would be more idiomatic.

column2: The rival is dominant.
column4: “实力很强势”搭配不自然；可以说“实力很强”或“很强势”。

column1: 对知识的爱好而言，我真的喜欢学汉字。
column2: In terms of intellectual hobbies, I really like learning Chinese characters.
column4: “对知识的爱好而言” is unnatural phrasing in Chinese.

column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” does not translate “寺里很安静” (“It’s quiet in the temple”).

column2: A big event in the neighborhood.
column4: “A big event in the neighborhood” is a sentence fragment.

column2: Be careful. That's an expensive piece of equipment.
column4: 这个 means “this,” but the English says “that.”

column1: 小明看场电影哭了一个小时。
column2: Xiaoming cried for an hour while watching the movie.
column4: “看场电影哭了一个小时” is awkward; it should say something like “看电影的时候哭了一个小时.”

column1: 就像食物喂养身体，所以阅读喂养心灵。
column2: Just as food feeds the body, so reading feeds the mind.
column4: “喂养心灵” is an unnatural way to express that reading nourishes the mind.

column2: The roof leaks in 3 different places.
column4: “三处在漏” is unnatural here; say “屋顶有三处漏水”.

column2: Data shows on the screen.
column4: “Data shows on the screen” is unnatural; the screen displays the data.

column2: The hillside is a big slope.
column4: “山坡是一个大坡” sounds unnatural and redundant; “这个山坡很大” is more natural.

column2: The work made new progress.
column4: “The work made new progress” is unnatural; say “There has been new progress on the work.”

column2: I do all the work.
column4: “都全” is redundant here; use “工作都由我做” or “工作全都由我做”.

column2: The factory output many products.
column4: The past-tense verb should be “outputted” or “produced,” not “output.”

column2: How will the project work?
column4: “工程要怎么见效” is an unnatural phrasing; the sentence would need to be reworded to ask how the project will produce results.

column1: 己经晚了，所以我回了家。
column2: It was already late, so I went back home.
column4: “己经” uses the wrong character; it should be “已经.”

column1: 已婚的人有时候希望他们是单身，。
column2: Married people sometimes wish they were single.
column4: The Chinese has malformed punctuation: the comma before the final period is unnecessary.

column1: 已经十一点了他还没来。
column2: It's eleven and he's not coming.
column4: “还没来” means he hasn’t arrived yet; “he’s not coming” suggests he won’t come.

column2: Twenty years already passed.
column4: In this context, English needs “Twenty years have already passed.”

column1: 希望别破妈妈发现才好。
column2: I hope Mom doesn't find out.
column4: “别破妈妈发现” is ungrammatical; it should be “别被妈妈发现.”

column1: 希望我们有机会再合作。
column2: Hope we can do business again someday.
column4: “再合作” means cooperate again; “do business again” is narrower and adds a business context.

column2: Fuck you!
column4: This is an offensive insult.

column2: Good job!
column4: 这里应写“干得好”，不是“干的好”。

column2: There are many fields on the plain.
column4: The Chinese says the plain is flat and has no mountains; it does not say there are many fields.

column2: An average of 10,000 steps a day.
column4: Both versions are sentence fragments, with no subject or context.

column1: 年轻人很喜欢用像支付宝之类的电子支付方式。
column2: Young people love using electronic methods of payment like Alipay and similar.
column4: “And similar” is unnatural here; say “and similar methods” or “and the like.”

column1: 广大读者喜欢这本杂志。
column2: The broad readership loves this magazine.
column4: “The broad readership” is an awkward expression here; “Readers love this magazine” is more natural.

column1: 广泛的安全措施实施了。
column2: Broad safety measures were put into effect.
column4: “广泛的安全措施实施了” is awkwardly phrased; the Chinese is not natural.

column2: It would be nice to have a party.
column4: “开个聚会” is not a natural way to say “have a party”; use “办个聚会” or “开个派对”.

column2: Begin the launch countdown.
column4: “开始发射倒数” is not a natural way to say this; use “开始发射倒计时” or “开始倒数发射.”

column2: Getting started was difficult.
column4: 开始很难 describes starting as difficult; it does not say that getting started was difficult in the past.

column2: drive very fast
column4: Both sides are verb phrases, not complete sentences.

column2: happily laugh
column4: Both sides are verb phrases, not complete sentences.

column2: Drive safely.
column4: “保安全” is an unnatural way to say this; “开车要注意安全” is more idiomatic.

column1: 当听到这个消息她看起来高兴。
column2: She looks happy on hearing the news.
column4: The Chinese is awkward; say “听到这个消息时，她看起来很高兴”.

column1: 当她回来的时后，我就离开。
column2: I'll leave when she comes back.
column4: “时后” is an incorrect character; it should be “时候.”

column1: 当我们离开的时候，谁来照顾狗？
column2: Who will take care of the dog while we are away?
column4: “当我们离开的时候” refers to when we leave; “while we are away” refers to the period after we have left.

column2: There was only three people at that time.
column4: “There was only three people” should be “There were only three people.”

column1: 当时我没想到这个问题。
column2: During that time I didn't expect to have a problem.
column4: 中文说当时没想到这个问题，英文却说没预料到会有问题。

column1: 当汽车爆炸时，车上只有三名乘客。
column2: There were only three passengers on the bus when it exploded.
column4: 汽车 means car, while the English says bus.

column2: It's cold around now in past years.
column4: “in past years”不自然；可说“It's cold around this time in previous years.”

column2: I'll square things with you later.
column4: “Square things with you” suggests settling a dispute, not simply talking later.

column1: 很多人住在我们的附近。
column2: There are many people living near us.
column4: “住在我们的附近”不自然；通常说“住在我们附近”。

column1: 很多人士都来参加了典礼。
column2: People from all walks attended the ceremony.
column4: “People from all walks” is an incomplete, unnatural version of “people from all walks of life” and does not accurately translate 很多人士.

column1: 很多外国人爱中国文化。
column2: placeholder
column4: “Placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: It was easy to fix.
column4: “很好修”表示容易修理，英文的“It was easy to fix”明确说的是过去。

column2: It'll clear up soon.
column4: “放睛” is a wrong character; the standard phrase is “放晴”.

column2: The electricity came on again in a few minutes.
column4: “很快” means “soon,” not specifically “in a few minutes.”

column2: I'm glad to see you back.
column4: “见到你” means see you again; “see you back” suggests you have returned.

column2: I'm glad to see you back.
column4: 再见到您 means “see you again”; it does not say that you have returned.

column1: 志愿者们宣传环保知识。
column2: Volunteers publicize eco knowledge.
column4: “Eco knowledge” is not a natural English phrase; “knowledge about environmental protection” would be clearer.

column2: Quick, help me!
column4: “快救命啊” is not a natural way to call for help; “快来救命啊” or “救命啊，快！” would be more natural.

column1: 快要考期末试了，所以我很忙。
column2: I'm busy because the finals are drawing on.
column4: “The finals are drawing on” is not natural English; say “the finals are approaching.”

column2: Hurry, or we'll be late.
column4: “要不然迟到” implies the person being addressed will be late, but “we'll be late” changes the subject.

column2: The courier picks up tomorrow.
column4: “Picks up” needs an object here; the English sentence is incomplete.

column2: Don't you know how?
column4: The Chinese means “How come you don’t know?”; the English asks whether the person knows how to do something.

column1: 总之，我们这么做都是为了孩子好。
column4: The English translation is missing.

column2: The general meeting began at 9 am on the dot.
column4: 总会 and 开始了 do not fit together here, making the sentence ungrammatical.

column2: Are you students?
column4: “您们” is not natural Mandarin; use “你们” or “您各位”.

column2: You're the best.
column4: “您太好了”通常是“You're so kind/good of you”，不等于“You're the best.”

column1: 您应遵循你老师的建议。
column2: You should follow your teacher's advice.
column4: The sentence mixes the polite 您 with 你; use one form consistently.

column1: 您想去电影院还是去剧院吗？
column2: Do you want to go to the cinema or the theater?
column4: The question particle 吗 is unnatural with an either-or question; say 你想去电影院还是去剧院？

column1: 您是在这儿用餐，还是给您打包带走？
column2: Are you going to eat here or do you want us to wrap it?
column4: “打包带走” means packing it to take away, which the English “wrap it” does not express.

column1: 您知道这附近有便宜的旅馆吗？
column2: Would you know a cheap hotel in the near?
column4: “In the near” is not natural English; say “nearby” or “in the area.”

column1: 您能用英语沟通您想要说的话吗？
column2: Can you communicate in English what you want to say?
column4: “沟通您想要说的话”不自然；更自然的说法是“用英语表达您想说的话”。

column2: How do you like your eggs done?
column4: The Chinese asks what kind of eggs you want, not how you want them cooked.

column2: What do you think she can do?
column4: 会做什么 asks what she will do, not what she is able to do.

column2: The situation is urgent.
column4: “情况很迫切” is an unnatural collocation; “情况很紧迫” is more natural.

column2: Imagine!
column4: “想一想” means “think about it,” not “imagine.”

column1: 想到自己的未来，她不安起来。
column2: Thinking about her future, she is unsettled.
column4: “不安起来” means she became unsettled, while the English describes her as currently unsettled.

column2: Want to know?
column4: This is a context-dependent fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column1: 意外中有十个人受了伤。
column2: Ten people were injured in the accident.
column4: “意外中” is unnatural here; say “事故中” or “意外事故中.”

column2: It is kind of you go out of your way to help me.
column4: “It is kind of you go out of your way” is ungrammatical; it should be “It is kind of you to go out of your way.”

column2: Do good to those who hate you.
column4: The Chinese says “Thank those who hate you,” not “Do good to those who hate you.”

column2: May the force be with you.
column4: “大能” is not a natural translation of “the Force”; “原力” is the established term.

column2: slowly walk
column4: Both sides are verb phrases, not complete sentences.

column1: 戏法人人会变，各有巧妙不同。
column2: Everyone's tricks are different; each differs in ingenious ways.
column4: The English is awkward and unnatural; it does not express the proverb naturally.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” does not translate the Chinese sentence.

column2: Scores rose a few points.
column4: “百分点” means percentage points, not simply points.

column2: I must've mistyped the number.
column4: “打错号码” means dialing the wrong number, not necessarily mistyping it.

column1: 我一把孩子抱在手里，他就开始哭了。
column2: The moment I held the baby in my arms, it began to cry.
column4: “抱在手里” is unnatural here; a native speaker would usually say “抱在怀里”.

column2: I don't know a single thing.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker knows no news or information, not that they don't know a single thing about anything.

column2: I was expecting it!
column4: “我一直在期待着” means “I've been looking forward to it,” while “I was expecting it” describes an expectation in the past.

column2: I am online.
column4: 我上网了 means “I went/got online,” not “I am online.”

column1: 我下周四前要这份工作。
column2: I want this work done by next Thursday.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker wants or needs this job; the English says they want a piece of work completed.

column2: I wouldn't try that again.
column4: “我不会再试了” means “I won’t try again,” not “I wouldn’t try that again.”

column1: 我不会写繁体字，但我可以读。
column2: I cannot write traditional characters, but I am fine reading them.
column4: “我可以读”表示有能力阅读；“I'm fine reading them”不明确表达这种能力。

column2: I don't think I agree.
column4: “我不同意” directly means “I disagree”; the English adds uncertainty or hesitation.

column2: I hate drinking soup.
column4: “不喜欢” means “don’t like,” which is weaker than “hate.”

column1: 我不喜欢她，因为她不友好。
column2: I don't like her because she is very unfriendly.
column4: “不友好” means “not friendly,” not necessarily “very unfriendly.”

column1: 我不在讨论这个问题的状态。
column2: I am not in a situation to discuss this problem.
column4: “我不在讨论这个问题的状态” is not a natural way to say you are not in a position to discuss the problem.

column2: I shouldn't have logged off.
column4: The Chinese says he shouldn't log out, while the English says he shouldn't have logged off in the past.

column2: I didn't mean to.
column4: 我不想是“我不想要／不愿意”，不是“我不是故意的”。

column1: 我不想一个人过情人节。
column2: I didn't want to be alone on Valentine's Day.
column4: The Chinese says “I don’t want to be alone,” not “I didn’t want to be alone.”

column2: I don't want to eat again.
column4: 我不想再吃了 means “I don’t want to eat any more”; “eat again” suggests eating on another occasion.

column2: I didn't want to get up early.
column4: The Chinese says “I don’t want to get up early,” not “I didn’t want to.”

column2: I didn't mean to discourage you.
column4: 打击你的 is incomplete and unnatural here; it should be 打击你.

column2: I don't want to hurt you.
column4: The Chinese says you don't want to let the other person hurt someone; it doesn't say you don't want to hurt them.

column2: I didn't want to mislead anyone.
column4: 我不想 means “I don't want to”; the English says “I didn't want to.”

column2: I didn't want to say too much.
column4: 中文表示现在不想说太多，英文说的是过去不想说太多。

column1: 我不明白他为何搞这样。
column2: I have no idea why he did that.
column4: “搞这样” is not natural here; say “他为什么这样做” or “他为何这样做.”

column2: I don't see what he says.
column4: 他说的话 means what he said; “what he says” shifts the meaning to what he says generally or now.

column1: 我不明白这为什么是错的。
column2: I don't understand how it is wrong.
column4: 中文问为什么错，英文问错在哪里、如何错。

column1: 我不是个意愿自由主义着。
column2: I am not a libertarian.
column4: “意愿自由主义着” is not a natural or correct Chinese term for “libertarian.”

column2: I don't have to clean my room.
column4: The English adds “my”; the Chinese does not say whose room it is.

column1: 我不相信孩子能独自到东京。
column2: I don't believe the child came to Tokyo alone.
column4: 能独自到东京 means “can get to Tokyo alone,” not “came to Tokyo alone.”

column2: I don't believe in luck.
column4: “不相信幸运” is unnatural here; “不相信运气” is the natural way to say “don’t believe in luck.”

column1: 我不知道他为什么那样做？
column2: I wonder why he did that.
column4: 我不知道 means “I don’t know,” not “I wonder.”

column1: 我不知道我是否有足够多的钱。
column2: I don't know if my money is enough.
column4: “If my money is enough” is unnatural; say “if I have enough money.”

column2: I don't know if I still have it.
column4: 我不知道我还有没有 omits what the speaker still has, so it needs context not provided.

column1: 我不知道谁会在机场见我。
column2: I didn't know who was going to meet me at the airport.
column4: The Chinese says “I don't know”; the English says “I didn't know.”

column2: I don't know, nor do I care.
column4: “不想知道” means “don’t want to know,” not “don’t care.”

column1: 我不禁想我的儿子一直都在生。
column2: I cannot help thinking that my son is still alive.
column4: “一直都在生” is not a natural way to say “still alive”; use “一直都活着”.

column1: 我不能回答所有的问题。
column2: I couldn't answer all the questions.
column4: “不能” means “cannot,” while “couldn't” places the inability in the past.

column1: 我不能流利的用英文表达。
column2: I can't speak English fluently.
column4: “流利的” should be “流利地” when modifying “用英文表达”.

column2: I can make that happen.
column4: 我不能让那事发生 means “I can’t let that happen,” not “I can make that happen.”

column2: I don't think he is sincere.
column4: 诚实 means “honest,” not “sincere.”

column1: 我不觉得我可以相信他所说的。
column2: I don't feel like I can trust what he says.
column4: “我不觉得” means “I don’t think,” not “I don’t feel like.”

column2: I don't think you need to change.
column4: 该 means “should,” not “need to”; the English changes the meaning.

column1: 我不认为这件事让每个人都满意了。
column2: I don't think that anyone was satisfied.
column4: The Chinese says the matter did not satisfy everyone; the English says nobody was satisfied.

column2: I don't know him, who is he?
column4: The English joins two independent questions with a comma; use a period or question mark between them.

column2: I couldn't remember ever having met her.
column4: The Chinese says “I don't remember,” not “I couldn't remember.”

column2: I don't feel like watching TV.
column4: “我不高兴看电视” means that watching TV makes me unhappy, not that I don’t feel like watching it.

column1: 我为我男朋友忘了情人节对他生气。
column2: I'm angry with my boyfriend for forgetting about Valentine's Day.
column4: The phrasing is ungrammatical. A natural version is “我因为我男朋友忘了情人节而生他的气。”

column1: 我为我的家人拍了照片。
column2: I took a picture of my family.
column4: “为我的家人拍了照片” more naturally means taking photos for my family, not taking a picture of them.

column1: 我乐意每年秋季去苹果园。
column2: I delight in going to the apple orchard each fall.
column4: “我乐意”通常表示愿意做某事；描述每年都喜欢去，更自然的说法是“我喜欢每年秋天去苹果园”。

column2: I also like it.
column4: “喜欢” has no stated object here, so translating it as “like it” requires context not provided.

column1: 我也很高兴能够认识你。
column2: I'm also very pleased to have seen you.
column4: “认识你” means getting to know or meeting you, not having seen you.

column2: I can come, too.
column4: “去” means “go”; the English says “come.”

column1: 我买了一个新的调色盘和几支水彩笔。
column2: I've bought a new palette and a few paint brushes.
column4: 水彩笔 are watercolor pens, not paint brushes.

column2: I bought a Daily News.
column4: “A Daily News” is awkward English for a copy of a newspaper; say “a copy of the Daily News” or “a daily newspaper.”

column2: I buy flowers.
column4: “我买的花” is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence, and does not mean “I buy flowers.”

column2: I was late for school this morning.
column4: 描述今天早上已经发生的事，通常说“我今天早上上学迟到了”。

column2: I have an audition today.
column4: 面试 means a job interview, not an audition.

column1: 我今年去了好几次外国。
column2: I have been abroad several times this year.
column4: “去了好几次外国” is unnatural; a native speaker would more likely say “去了好几次国外” or “去了好几个外国.”

column1: 我仍然热爱著网球运动。
column2: I am still keeping up my tennis craze.
column4: “Keeping up my tennis craze” is not a natural way to express still loving tennis.

column2: I come from a large family.
column4: 我从一个大家庭来 is unnatural; a native speaker would say 我来自一个大家庭.

column1: 我从两点开始写呀写呀，一分钟也没休息过。
column2: I have been writing since two o'clock without a break.
column4: “写呀写呀” is unnatural in this sentence; “一直写” would be more natural.

column2: I heard from him.
column4: The Chinese means “I heard it from him,” while “I heard from him” usually means he contacted or communicated with me.

column2: I'm constantly studying.
column4: 我从早学到晚 means “I study from morning till night,” not “I’m constantly studying.”

column1: 我从没听说他关于其他人说坏话。
column2: I have never heard him speak ill of others.
column4: “听说他关于其他人说坏话” is an unnatural construction; say “听说他说别人的坏话”.

column2: I'd never say something like that.
column4: “我从没说过”表示从未说过；“I'd never say”表达的是不会说或不愿说。

column2: I've never been so proud of you.
column4: “这么以你为豪”语序不自然；可说“从没这么为你感到自豪”。

column1: 我以前每天早上也会去散步。
column2: I used to take a walk every morning.
column4: The Chinese says they also used to take a walk every morning; “also” is missing from the English.

column2: I used to feel it dull.
column4: “I used to feel it dull”不自然；可说“I used to find it dull”。

column1: 我们一直是很好的炮友。
column2: We were always very good fuck buddies.
column4: “一直是” does not specify that the relationship was only in the past; “were always” does.

column1: 我们上个星期去了数学的考试。
column2: We took an examination in math last week.
column4: “去了数学的考试” is not a natural way to say this; use “参加了数学考试” or “去考数学.”

column1: 我们上课时学了九的根是三。
column2: We learned at school that the square root of nine is three.
column4: “九的根是三” is not a natural way to express “the square root of nine is three”; say “九的平方根是三” or “九的根号是三”.

column2: We don't do it.
column4: “我们不做这样” is ungrammatical; say “我们不这样做”.

column1: 我们不应该把金钱看得太重。
column2: We should not make too much of money.
column4: “Make too much of money” is unnatural English; say “attach too much importance to money.”

column1: 我们不知道他会不会来。
column2: We don't know whether he can come or not.
column4: “会不会来” asks whether he will come, not whether he can come.

column1: 我们之间已经没有感情了。
column2: I don't like him any more than he likes me.
column4: The Chinese says there are no feelings left between us; the English makes a comparison of how much two people like each other.

column1: 我们也都没吃饭，一起去吧。
column2: We all haven't eaten either. Let's go together.
column4: “We all haven't eaten either” is awkward and can be read as saying not everyone has eaten. “None of us have eaten either” is natural.

column2: We're used to eating plain food.
column4: 习惯简单的食物不自然；更自然的说法是“习惯吃简单的食物”。

column2: We exchanged cards.
column4: 名片 means “business cards,” not cards in general.

column1: 我们从前从没有过这个问题。
column2: We've never had this problem before.
column4: “从前从没有过” is awkward; a natural phrasing is “从前从来没有过这个问题。”

column2: Let's break off, shall we?
column4: “休息一下” means take a break; “break off” usually means stop something abruptly.

column1: 我们使用了强大的措施来预防。
column2: We took strong measures to prevent it.
column4: “强大的措施”搭配不自然；通常说“有力的措施”。

column2: We both drive sports cars.
column4: “驾跑车” is not the natural verb choice here; say “开跑车” or “驾驶跑车”。

column2: We couldn't do it.
column4: 做不到 usually means “can't do it”; “couldn't” places it in the past.

column2: We are firstly going to Beijing.
column4: “We are firstly going to Beijing” is unnatural English. “We are going to Beijing first” is natural.

column2: We just now cleaned the toilet.
column4: “We just now cleaned” is unnatural English; say “We just cleaned the toilet.”

column1: 我们到了火车站的时候，火车已经开出了。
column2: The train had already left when we got to station.
column4: The English should say “when we got to the station.”

column2: We go to the South of France for a change of air.
column4: “For a change of air” is unnatural English; “to get a change of scenery” or “to unwind” would be natural.

column1: 我们去考察当地的风俗。
column2: We survey the local customs.
column4: “去考察” means to go and study/investigate; the English omits the going.

column2: We made fun of him about this.
column4: “取笑了他这一点” is awkward. A natural phrasing would be “我们因为这件事取笑了他。”

column2: We can.
column4: “我们可以” is an incomplete response without context specifying what you can do.

column1: 我们可以在二月二十八日三时左右见面吗？
column2: Can we meet February 28, around 3:00 pm?
column4: The Chinese says around three o’clock without specifying a.m. or p.m.; the English adds p.m.

column2: We probably should've left early.
column4: The Chinese suggests leaving early, while “should've left” places it in the past.

column2: We had a delicious meal.
column4: “吃了一顿美食” is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “吃了一顿好吃的” or “享用了一顿美食”。

column2: We took a walk in the park.
column4: The Chinese describes a present or habitual walk, but the English says it happened in the past.

column1: 我们在学校有一个早午餐。
column2: We had an early lunch at school.
column4: The Chinese says “we have” a brunch, not “we had” one.

column1: 我们在晚上九点时吃晚餐。
column2: We have our evening meal at 9 here.
column4: The English adds “here,” which is not stated in the Chinese.

column1: 我们在火车上十个小时。
column2: We were on the train for ten hours.
column4: The Chinese is missing a verb or other wording to express being on the train for ten hours; e.g. 我们在火车上待了十个小时。

column1: 我们如同无限般的使用地球的能源资源。
column2: We have used earth's energy resources as if they were limitless.
column4: “如同无限般的使用” is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “像资源无限一样使用”.

column1: 我们学校很少办才艺比赛之类的活动。
column2: Our school rarely holds activities like talent shows or similar.
column4: “Or similar” is unnatural here; say “or similar activities” or “and the like.”

column2: There are a lot of cute guys in our school.
column4: 帅哥 means “handsome guys,” not “cute guys.”

column1: 我们定期在这里施行安全检查。
column2: We conduct safety inspections here on a regular basis.
column4: “施行安全检查” is an unnatural collocation; “进行安全检查” is natural.

column1: 我们已经将它做了分析。
column2: We've had it analyzed.
column4: “将它做了分析”搭配不自然；可以说“对它进行了分析”。

column2: We all don't have money anymore.
column4: “We all don't have money anymore” is awkward; “We don't have any money left” is natural.

column1: 我们并没有完全断了你的后路。
column2: We're not terminating you.
column4: The Chinese says you haven't completely cut off someone's options, not that you're not terminating them.

column2: We're not terminating you.
column4: “赶尽杀绝” means to wipe someone out completely, not to terminate someone.

column2: We have what we need.
column4: “我们应有尽有” means “We have everything”; it does not mean only that we have what we need.

column2: We had a party.
column4: “开了一个聚会” is unnatural here; say “办了一个聚会” or “举行了一个聚会.”

column1: 我们很快就到这儿了，不是吗？
column2: We arrived here fast, didn't we?
column4: 这儿了 indicates that you'll be here soon, not that you arrived here quickly.

column1: 我们很穷，不过我们过的很快乐。
column2: We are poor, but we are happy.
column4: 这里应写“过得很快乐”，表示状态时用“得”，不是“的”。

column2: We're on our own.
column4: The Chinese says we have to rely on ourselves; “we’re on our own” does not express that obligation.

column1: 我们得到了我们想要的。
column2: We've got what we need.
column4: 想要的 means “what we wanted,” not “what we need.”

column1: 我们所有的老师都很年轻并且喜爱教学。
column2: All our teachers were young and loved teaching.
column4: The Chinese describes the teachers as young and fond of teaching, while the English puts both in the past.

column1: 我们是大人，不是小孩儿。
column2: We're men, not boys.
column4: “大人，不是小孩儿” means adults, not children; it does not specify men or boys.

column2: We'll talk about this later.
column4: “晚会” means an evening party or gala; it doesn’t naturally mean “later.”

column2: We had two apples.
column4: “有” says they have two apples; “had” makes it past possession.

column1: 我们有在这里停车的许可。
column2: We got permission to park here.
column4: “有许可” means have permission, not that permission was obtained.

column2: We try.
column4: 我们来试试 means “Let’s try,” not “We try.”

column1: 我们的价值就是采访、分析以及组合投资管理人。
column2: Our value lies in conducting interviews, analysis, as well as synthesizing and managing investment portfolios.
column4: “采访、分析以及组合投资管理人” is not a natural parallel list in Chinese.

column2: Our country grows stronger day by day.
column4: “富强” means prosperous and powerful, but the English only says “stronger.”

column1: 我们的山不怎么高，你们的高多了。
column2: Our mountains aren't really very high. Yours are much bigger.
column4: 高多了 means much taller/higher, not much bigger.

column1: 我们的房子前有一个园。
column2: There is a garden in front of the house.
column4: “一个园” is unnatural here; “一个花园” is the usual phrasing.

column1: 我们的房子去年夏天遭到闯入。
column2: Our house was broken into last summer.
column4: “房子遭到闯入” is unidiomatic; say “房子被闯入” or “房子遭人闯入”。

column1: 我们的晚饭要晚点吃了。
column2: We'll be late for dinner.
column4: The Chinese says dinner will be later, while “We'll be late for dinner” usually means arriving late to dinner.

column2: Ours has come.
column4: 我们的 needs an understood noun or referent (for example, “ours”); without context, it is unclear what has come.

column2: our teacher
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column2: There goes our bus.
column4: 车 does not specify a bus; the English adds that detail.

column2: our money
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column1: 我们穿过了一条人来人往的街道。
column2: We came through a busy street.
column4: 穿过 here means “crossed,” not “came through.”

column1: 我们第一次参观了他的家乡。
column2: We visited his home country for the first time.
column4: “家乡” means “hometown,” not “home country.”

column1: 我们等了一会儿，但是没等到他。
column2: We waited a bit, but he didn't come.
column4: 没等到他 means they didn't manage to wait until or meet him; it doesn't necessarily mean he didn't come.

column1: 我们算计着改革生产流程。
column2: We are planning changes to the manufacturing process.
column4: “算计着改革生产流程” is unnatural here; “算计” does not naturally mean planning changes to a process.

column2: We date to watch a movie.
column4: “We date to watch a movie” is unnatural English.

column2: We often exchange experience.
column4: “Exchange experience” is awkward here; “exchange experiences” is more natural.

column1: 我们花一万二千元买了这辆车。
column2: We bought this car for 12,000.
column4: The Chinese specifies 12,000 yuan, but the English leaves out the currency.

column2: We are going to take an airplane to go to the USA.
column4: “Take an airplane to go to” is awkward and redundant; say “take a plane to the USA.”

column1: 我们试图让手指互相交错。
column2: We kept our fingers crossed.
column4: 中文说试着让手指交错，英文的“kept our fingers crossed”通常表示希望好运。

column2: We still have a chance.
column4: “还有次机会” is missing “一”; the natural phrase is “还有一次机会.”

column1: 我们这周末应该干点什么的。
column2: We should do something this weekend.
column4: The final “的” is awkward here; say “我们这周末应该干点什么.”

column2: We all quite miss you.
column4: “We all quite miss you” is unnatural English; “We all miss you quite a bit” is more idiomatic.

column1: 我们都是打工的，不得不服从公司的安排。
column2: We all employees here. We have to follow what the company has decided.
column4: “We all employees here” is ungrammatical; it needs a verb such as “are.”

column2: None of us has ever been on a airplane before.
column4: “A airplane” is ungrammatical; it should be “an airplane.”

column2: We all breathed a big sigh of relief.
column4: “舒了一口长气” is not a natural collocation; say “长长地舒了一口气”。

column2: My team is always losing.
column4: 我们队 means “our team,” not “my team.”

column1: 我们随著她的音乐起舞吧。
column2: Let's dance to her song.
column4: “音乐” means music, while “song” is more specific.

column2: I'd be glad to do that for you.
column4: “我会乐意帮你做” is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “我很乐意帮你做.”

column1: 我会向你全部解释清楚的。
column2: I'll explain everything to you.
column4: “向你全部解释清楚” has awkward word order; say “我会把一切都向你解释清楚”.

column2: I'll tell him you asked.
column4: “你来问过” means you came to ask; the English omits that detail.

column1: 我会告诉你去车站的路。
column2: I'll show you to the station.
column4: “告诉你去车站的路”是告诉你怎么去，不是陪你去车站。

column2: I'll be back by seven or eight o'clock.
column4: “在七八点回家” means coming home around seven or eight, not necessarily by then.

column1: 我会把所有有用的信息提供给您的。
column2: I will provide you all the necessary information.
column4: 中文说“有用的信息”，英文说“necessary information”（必要的信息），意思不同。

column2: I'll come to your place.
column4: “来你的地方” sounds unnatural here; “来你那儿” or “去你那里” would be more natural.

column2: I'll work as long as I live.
column4: “我会活到老工作到老” is awkward; a more natural phrasing is “我会一直工作到老。”

column2: I'll get you something nice.
column4: The word order is unnatural; say “我会给你好东西” or “我会给你点好东西.”

column2: I'll keep it.
column4: 我会记下来 means “I’ll write it down” or “I’ll note it down,” not “I’ll keep it.”

column2: I can talk for a bit.
column4: 我会说一点儿 means “I can speak a little,” not “I can talk for a bit.”

column2: I'll get some help.
column4: 我会需要帮助 means “I will need help,” not “I'll get some help.”

column1: 我住了一个星期的医院。
column2: I spent a week in hospital.
column4: “住了一个星期的医院” is unnatural; say “在医院住了一个星期.”

column2: I'm alive in Tokyo.
column4: 我住在东京 means “I live in Tokyo,” not “I’m alive in Tokyo.”

column1: 我儿子不在家，他在学校。
column2: My son is not at home, he is at school.
column4: The English joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

column2: I eat up everything!
column4: “我全吃光！” expresses a one-time action or intention, not the habitual “I eat up everything!”

column2: I know all that.
column4: “我全知道” is not a natural way to say “I know all that”; say “我都知道” or “我全都知道”.

column2: I got up about six.
column4: 我六点左右起床 describes a usual or general waking time, not a past event.

column2: I miswrote a word.
column4: “miswrote a word”不自然；可以说“I wrote a character incorrectly”或“I wrote the wrong character”。

column2: I'm freezing!
column4: “我冰死了”不是自然的说法；应说“我冻死了”。

column2: I only happened to pass here just now.
column4: “Only happened to” adds the idea that passing by was incidental; the Chinese just says the speaker passed by here a moment ago.

column2: I just met her ten days ago.
column4: 我刚认识她十天 means “I’ve only known her for ten days,” not “I met her ten days ago.”

column2: It was two months ago that I arrived in Tokyo.
column4: “我到东京是两个月前” is unnatural; say “我是两个月前到东京的.”

column1: 我前男友不再住在这个城市了。
column2: My ex-husband no longer lives in this city.
column4: “前男友” means ex-boyfriend, not ex-husband.

column1: 我办完事会立刻联络你。
column2: I'll call you as soon as I've finished.
column4: “联络你” means “contact you” and does not necessarily mean calling by phone.

column1: 我努力劝他远离那个计划，但是他不听。
column2: I tried to talk him out of the project, but in vain.
column4: 劝他远离那个计划 is unnatural for persuading someone not to do a project; say 劝他放弃那个计划.

column2: I met him at Tokyo Station.
column4: The Chinese says “I’m going to Tokyo Station to meet him,” not “I met him at Tokyo Station.”

column2: I'm going to work.
column4: 我去工作 is not the natural way to say “I'm going to work”; 我去上班 is more idiomatic.

column1: 我去年动了青光眼手术。
column2: I had an operation for glaucoma last year.
column4: “动了青光眼手术” is not a natural collocation; say “做了青光眼手术” or “动手术治疗青光眼.”

column1: 我发现一个地方能买到便宜的水果。
column2: I've found a place to buy cheaper fruits.
column4: “Cheaper” adds a comparison that is not expressed by 便宜.

column1: 我发现他就是会很晚才来这样的人。
column2: I find that it's typical for him to come too late.
column4: “就是会很晚才来这样的人” is an unnatural construction; “就是那种总是很晚才来的人” would be more natural.

column2: I'm fed up with fast food.
column4: “我受够吃快餐了” is not a natural construction. Say “我受够了吃快餐” or “我吃快餐吃够了。”

column2: I just want to be happy.
column4: “我只想高兴” is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say “我只想开心”.

column2: I just didn't want you in here.
column4: The Chinese expresses not wanting someone to come in, while the English puts that in the past.

column2: I just want him to be happy.
column4: “想要他开心”不自然；更自然的说法是“我只是想让他开心”。

column1: 我只是想试着快乐的生活而已。
column2: I'm just trying to live a happy life, that's all.
column4: “快乐的生活” is unnatural in this construction; say “快乐地生活” or “过快乐的生活.”

column1: 我只能走路，因为打不到出租车。
column2: There are no taxis, so I must walk.
column4: 打不到出租车 means you can’t get a taxi; it doesn’t necessarily mean there are no taxis.

column2: My name's Cyril. Nice to meet you.
column4: 你好 means “hello,” not specifically “nice to meet you.”

column2: My name is 王明.
column4: Using the Chinese characters 王明 in this English sentence is unnatural; the name would normally be written “Wang Ming.”

column1: 我可以给我的家庭提供衣食。
column2: I can provide my family with food and clothing.
column4: 给我的家庭提供衣食 is unnatural; a native speaker would more naturally say 给家人提供衣食.

column2: I don't eat chicken skin.
column4: 我吃不下 means “I can’t eat,” not “I don’t eat.”

column2: I ate them.
column4: The Chinese does not specify an object; “them” is added in the English.

column2: I've eaten it.
column4: 我吃过了 means “I’ve eaten” or “I’ve already eaten”; it does not specify “it.”

column2: I am supremely glad to hear it.
column4: “我听到这个非常开心” is awkwardly phrased; “听到这个我非常开心” is natural.

column1: 我听着听着歌，就唱起来了。
column2: As I listened and listened to the songs, I began to sing.
column4: “听着听着歌” is unnatural. Say “我听着听着歌就唱起来了” or “我听着听着就唱起歌来了。”

column2: I heard my name called.
column4: 我听见有人叫我 means “I heard someone call me”; it does not specifically say they called the speaker’s name.

column1: 我告诉了你停下来，不是吗？
column2: I told you to stop, didn't I?
column4: “告诉了你停下来” is unnatural here; “我叫你停下来” is the natural way to say “I told you to stop.”

column2: I told you to get out.
column4: “告诉”通常不能直接接这个命令；说“我叫过你出去”或“我告诉过你要出去”更自然。

column2: I am nearly as tall as she.
column4: “近一样高”不自然；可以说“差不多一样高”或“几乎一样高”。

column1: 我哥哥有时会教我做功课。
column2: My brother sometimes helps me with my homework.
column4: 教我做功课 means “teaches me to do my homework,” not simply “helps me with my homework.”

column2: I like to eat hot soup.
column4: 中文说“喝汤”（drink soup），英文说“eat soup”。

column2: I like the green colour.
column4: “绿颜色” is unnatural here; say “我喜欢绿色。”

column2: I've enjoyed reading this novel.
column4: The Chinese says “I like reading this novel,” not that you have enjoyed reading it.

column1: 我回答您之前要好好考虑一下。
column2: I will need to think for a while before I answer you.
column4: 好好考虑一下 means to think it over carefully, not necessarily to think for a while.

column2: Our country abounds in products.
column4: 物产 refers to a country’s natural resources or produce, not “products” in the usual English sense.

column2: I went to college in Shanghai.
column4: 我在上海上大学 means the speaker is attending college in Shanghai, not that they went there in the past.

column2: I ate it once two years ago.
column4: “在两年前” is unnatural here; say “我两年前吃过一次。”

column1: 我在中学学习，弟弟在小学。
column2: I study in middle school, my brother in primary school.
column4: The second clause is missing a verb; say “and my brother is in primary school.”

column1: 我在你的生日会送给你一辆自行车。
column2: I will give you a bicycle for your birthday.
column4: The Chinese says the gift is given at your birthday party; the English says it is for your birthday.

column1: 我在找有我尺寸的上衣。
column2: I'm looking for a coat in my size.
column4: “上衣” means an upper-body garment or top, not specifically a coat.

column2: I spent my vacation at the beach.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker is vacationing at the beach; the English places the vacation in the past.

column2: I'm saving up to buy a new car.
column4: “我在省钱买新车”不自然；通常说“我在攒钱买新车”。

column1: 我在窗户上看见了我的映像。
column2: I saw my reflection in the window.
column4: “映像” is not a natural way to refer to a reflection here; “倒影” would be more idiomatic.

column1: 我在自己家中哪里都不能读书，那里太吵了。
column2: At my house, I have nowhere to study - it's too noisy there.
column4: “在自己家中哪里都不能读书” is awkward; a native speaker would more naturally say “在自己家里哪儿都没法学习.”

column1: 我在街上遇到我的老师。
column2: I greet my teacher on the street.
column4: “遇到” means encountered or ran into, not greeted.

column1: 我在那一个观点上同意他。
column2: I agree with him on that point.
column4: “在那一个观点上同意他”不自然；可说“在那一点上我同意他”。

column1: 我在那商店花低价买了台录像机。
column2: I bought a VCR at that store for a low price.
column4: “花低价买” is unnatural; say “以低价买” or “花很低的价钱买”.

column2: I'm sitting here in my car.
column4: 英文多出了“here”，中文没有表达“这里”。

column2: I arrived here about five o'clock.
column4: 中文通常表示“我大概五点到这里”（将来到达），而英文说的是已经到达。

column2: I'm too happy!
column4: “太高兴了” expresses great happiness; “too happy” suggests excessive happiness.

column1: 我女儿昨天十二点才睡觉，作业太多了。
column2: My daughter didn't go to bed until 12 o'clock yesterday. Too much homework.
column4: “Too much homework” is a sentence fragment; the Chinese gives the reason her daughter went to bed late.

column2: my girlfriend's company
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a sentence.

column1: 我奶奶也告诉了我这样。
column2: My grandmother told me so.
column4: 我奶奶也告诉了我这样 is unnatural; say 我奶奶也这么告诉我.

column2: I mean to fight hard.
column4: 好想打架 means “really want to fight,” not “mean to fight hard.”

column2: I would rather you had a day off.
column4: The Chinese expresses a preference for the person to take a day off, not that they had one in the past.

column1: 我完全记不起你的名字了。
column2: I quite forget your name.
column4: “I quite forget your name” is unnatural English; say “I completely forgot your name” or “I can’t remember your name at all.”

column1: 我对你太了解了，我都能知道你下一步要做什么。
column2: I know you too well. I can even tell what your next move will be.
column4: “我都能知道” is unnatural here; “我都能猜到” would be more idiomatic.

column2: She attracted me at first sight.
column4: The Chinese says “I fell in love with her at first sight,” while the English says she attracted me.

column2: I don't feel sorry for her.
column4: “我对她毫无歉意” means feeling no remorse or having no apology toward her, not feeling no pity for her.

column2: I was entirely bummed out by the results.
column4: “Entirely bummed out” is an unnatural way to express being very disappointed.

column1: 我将确保你们在第一年后有一个增长。
column2: I'll see to it that you have a raise after the first year.
column4: “有一个增长” is unnatural here; a raise is usually expressed as “加薪” or “涨工资.”

column2: I just want to go!
column4: “我就要去” means “I’m going” or “I insist on going,” not simply “I just want to go.”

column2: I ran as fast as possible.
column4: The Chinese suggests running a little faster as far as possible, while the English says the speaker ran as fast as possible.

column2: I ran as fast as possible to catch up with her.
column4: “我尽快跑以赶上她” is unnatural; a more natural phrasing is “我尽可能快地跑，好赶上她。”

column2: I need it ASAP.
column4: “我尽快需要” is unnatural and lacks the thing needed; say “我尽快需要它” or “我急需它”.

column1: 我已经习惯了家门口过火车的声音了。
column2: I am used to hearing the train pass by my house.
column4: “家门口过火车的声音” is awkward; a more natural phrasing is “火车经过我家门口的声音”.

column1: 我已经受够了这个计划。
column2: I've had enough of this program.
column4: “计划”通常是“plan”，而“program”通常指程序、节目或课程。

column2: What more could I want?
column4: “我已经无欲无求了” means “I no longer want anything,” not “What more could I want?”

column2: I hope he hasn't had an accident.
column4: “他没发生意外” is an awkward collocation; a native speaker would more naturally say “他没出意外”.

column2: I hope that I'll see her.
column4: “我希望会看见她” is unnatural; say “我希望能见到她”.

column2: I wish you had told me this earlier.
column4: The English expresses regret about not being told earlier, while the Chinese does not clearly express that past regret.

column1: 我希望您快就会好起来。
column2: I hope you'll soon get well.
column4: “快就会好起来” is not natural here; say “很快就会好起来”.

column1: 我希望我没有得到职位。
column2: I wish that I hadn't taken the office.
column4: 我希望我没有得到职位 means “I wish I hadn’t gotten the position,” not that I hadn’t taken or accepted the office.

column2: I want to feel important.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker hopes others will value them, not simply that they want to feel important.

column1: 我希望更多人也能感受到。
column2: I wish more people felt the same way.
column4: 感受到 means to feel or experience something; it doesn’t necessarily mean feeling the same way.

column2: I wish to see my father.
column4: “看看我的父亲” sounds unnatural for wanting to see someone; “见见我父亲” is more natural.

column2: Shall I go for the doctor?
column4: “Go for the doctor” is not a natural way to ask whether you should see a doctor.

column2: I have to learn Japanese.
column4: “应该” means “should,” not “have to.”

column2: My younger brother just started working half a year ago.
column4: 我弟弟刚工作半年 means he has only been working for half a year, not that he started working half a year ago.

column1: 我很喜欢你为人设想的性格。
column2: I love how you think of other people's needs before your own.
column4: “你为人设想的性格” is unnatural; say “你为别人着想的性格” or “你替别人着想的样子。”

column1: 我很开心你不在我朋友卷里。
column2: I'm glad you're not in my circle of friends.
column4: “朋友卷” is incorrect here; the usual expression is “朋友圈”.

column1: 我很快乐能参加你的派对。
column2: I will be happy to attend your party.
column4: The Chinese says you are happy to be able to attend; the English says you will be happy to attend.

column1: 我很担心我作这份新工作就不会做得好。
column2: I am afraid that if I take this new job, I won't succeed at it.
column4: “作这份新工作” is not natural here; it should be “做这份新工作”.

column2: I was very relaxed.
column4: 我很放松 describes being relaxed now; “I was very relaxed” puts it in the past.

column2: I'm being patient.
column4: “我很有耐心” describes being patient in general; “I’m being patient” describes acting patiently now.

column1: 我得把手表调快两分钟。
column2: I need to set my watch to two minutes faster.
column4: “set my watch to two minutes faster”表达不自然；可说“set my watch two minutes ahead”。

column2: I had to stay at home.
column4: “我得留在家里” expresses a present or future obligation, not a past one.

column2: I must ask you to do just that.
column4: “我得问你做那件事” means I have to ask you about doing that, not ask you to do it.

column2: I have to write a bit.
column4: 写点什么 means to write something; “write a bit” usually means to write for a short time or in a small amount.

column1: 我必须在一小时内做完功课。
column2: I must finish my homework in an hour.
column4: “在一小时内”明确表示不超过一小时；“in an hour”也可表示一小时后。

column2: I must help my mother.
column4: “帮忙” does not take a direct object this way; say “帮我母亲” or “帮助我母亲”.

column1: 我想他得花两个小时才能把工作做完。
column2: It will take him two hours to finish the work.
column4: The Chinese says “I think” it will take him two hours; the English leaves that out.

column1: 我想你不会那么做的吧。
column2: I assume that you wouldn't want to do that.
column4: The Chinese suggests “I guess you won’t do that, right?”; it does not say you wouldn’t want to do it.

column1: 我想你表现我怎么做那个。
column2: I want you to show me how to do that.
column4: 表现我怎么做 is not natural Chinese here; use 示范给我看 or 教我怎么做.

column2: I want you to read this letter.
column4: “我想你读一下” is awkward; say “我想让你读一下这封信”.

column1: 我想准时到，就会准时到。
column2: I arrive precisely when I mean to.
column4: The Chinese says he wants to arrive on time and will do so; the English says he arrives when he chooses.

column2: I prefer to eat something else.
column4: “我想吃点别的” means “I want to eat something else,” not specifically “I prefer” it.

column1: 我想告诉你一个好消息。
column2: I want to tell you the good news.
column4: “一个好消息” means “some good news” or “a piece of good news”; “the good news” adds definiteness.

column1: 我想尽快从这个不透气的屋子里出去。
column2: I want to move out of this cramped room as soon as I can.
column4: 不透气 describes a stuffy or poorly ventilated room, and 出去 means get out; “cramped” and “move out” change the meaning.

column2: It must be around here somewhere.
column4: “我想应该” means “I think it should be,” which is less certain than “It must be.”

column2: I want you to come at once.
column4: “我想您马上来” is unnatural; “我希望您马上来” would be natural.

column2: I wanted to become a philosopher.
column4: 想通常 expresses a present desire; the English says “wanted,” which places it in the past.

column1: 我想我们还要再等半个小时。
column2: I would like to wait another half an hour.
column4: “我想” means “I think,” not “I would like.”

column2: I want a boyfriend.
column4: 我想男朋友 is not a natural way to say “I want a boyfriend”; say 我想要一个男朋友.

column2: I think it true.
column4: “I think it true” is ungrammatical; say “I think it’s true.”

column2: I want money.
column4: 我想钱 usually means “I think about money”; “I want money” is 我想要钱.

column1: 我感冒了，昨天便在床上睡觉。
column2: I caught a cold and was in bed yesterday.
column4: “昨天便在床上睡觉” is awkward here; “昨天就在床上休息” is more natural.

column2: I don't give a fuck about what you say!
column4: The Chinese says emphatically that the speaker won't listen; the English says they don't care and adds strong profanity.

column1: 我打算八点在房里吃早餐。
column2: I'd like breakfast in my room at 8 sharp.
column4: 我打算 means “I plan/intend to,” not “I’d like”; the English changes the meaning from a plan to a preference.

column1: 我找不到我三件套的背心。
column2: I can't find the waistcoat of my three piece suit.
column4: “我三件套的背心” is unnatural; a native speaker would say something like “我那套三件套西装的马甲.”

column2: I found you, didn't I?
column4: 我找到你了，没有么？ is not a natural tag question here; say 我找到你了，不是吗？

column1: 我承认我不知道怎么做。
column2: I admitted that I didn't know how to do that.
column4: The Chinese says “I admit,” but the English says “I admitted.”

column1: 我把我的新钢笔搞丢了。
column2: I've lost my new fountain pen.
column4: The English specifies a fountain pen, but the Chinese only says a new pen.

column2: I must decline.
column4: “我拒绝”是“I refuse/decline”，没有“必须”的意思。

column1: 我拿到了他还给我的钱。
column2: I got the money back from him.
column4: “我拿到了他还给我的钱”不自然；可说“我拿到了他还给我的钱”虽能理解，但更自然的是“我拿回了他还给我的钱”。

column1: 我收到了一个重要邮件。
column2: I received an important email.
column4: 邮件通常量词用“封”；“一个重要邮件”不自然。

column1: 我早上六时之前总是起不了床。
column2: It is difficult for me to get up before six.
column4: 中文说他总是没能在六点前起床，英文只说起床很困难。

column1: 我早就有感觉到这可能会发生。
column2: I had a feeling this might happen.
column4: “早就有感觉到”不自然；可以说“我早就感觉到这可能会发生”。

column2: I always drink milk with my breakfast.
column4: 一定会喝 means will definitely drink, not that she always drinks milk with breakfast.

column2: Tomorrow, I'm going to study at the library.
column4: “温习” means review, which is more specific than the English “study”.

column2: Tomorrow, I will book a dentist appointment.
column4: The Chinese specifies booking an appointment for a teeth cleaning; the English just says a dentist appointment.

column1: 我明天要去马德里，也就是西班牙的首都。
column2: Tomorrow, I want to go to Madrid. It is the capital city of Spain.
column4: “要去” expresses a plan or intention to go, not specifically wanting to go.

column2: I know how sad you are.
column4: “不幸” means unfortunate or unlucky, not necessarily sad.

column1: 我昨天玩了一晚上游戏。
column2: Yesterday, I played games all evening.
column4: “一晚上” means all night, while “all evening” is a shorter time span.

column2: I wrote a love letter last night.
column4: “情信” is not the usual Mandarin term for a love letter; “情书” is natural.

column2: I'm a free man.
column4: “Free man” specifies a male person, which the Chinese does not.

column2: I'm a computer scientist.
column4: “电脑科学家” is unnatural; “计算机科学家” is the usual term for “computer scientist.”

column2: I won't be wearing a tie.
column4: 系领带 means “tie a tie,” not “wear a tie.”

column2: I'm at university.
column4: 中文说“我是个大学生”，英文说的是“我在上大学”，意思不完全相同。

column2: I'm in this for the kids.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker came because of the children; the English says the children are the speaker’s motivation.

column1: 我是在北京学习的中文。
column2: It was in Beijing that I studied Chinese.
column4: 这个句子结构不自然。可以说“我是在北京学中文的”。

column1: 我是小孩子的时候，我是一样。
column2: I was like that when I was younger.
column4: “我是小孩子的时候，我是一样” is unnatural and incomplete; “我那时候也一样” would be natural.

column1: 我是据我所知最懒的人。
column2: I am the laziest person I know.
column4: “我是据我所知最懒的人”不自然；可说“我是我所认识的人里最懒的”。

column2: I'm atheist.
column4: “I'm atheist” is ungrammatical; it should be “I'm an atheist.”

column2: I'm Jewish.
column4: “我是犹太教” means “I am Judaism”; a person would say “我是犹太教徒.”

column2: I'm humble.
column4: 我是谦虚的不自然；通常说“我很谦虚”。

column2: I go to bed early at night.
column4: 我晚上睡觉很早 is unnatural word order; a natural phrasing is 我晚上很早睡觉.

column2: I prefer tea over coffee.
column4: “更喜欢茶喝咖啡”不合语法；应说“更喜欢茶而不是咖啡”或“比起咖啡更喜欢茶”。

column1: 我曾经想过当个太空物理学家。
column2: I once wanted to be an astrophysicist.
column4: “太空物理学家” means a space physicist, not specifically an astrophysicist.

column1: 我最不感兴趣的城市就是东京。
column2: Tokyo is the least attractive town to me.
column4: The Chinese says Tokyo is the city the speaker is least interested in, while the English says it is the least attractive.

column2: A good idea came to me.
column4: 我有一个好主意 means “I have a good idea,” not that an idea came to me.

column2: I have an egg.
column4: “一只蛋” is not a natural way to count an egg; say “一个鸡蛋” or “一颗蛋”.

column1: 我有不低于一千片光盘。
column2: I have no less than one thousand records.
column4: 光盘是 CDs/discs, not records.

column2: I had a neighbor who was blind.
column4: “我有个盲邻居” means “I have a blind neighbor,” not “I had” one.

column2: Am I pregnant?
column4: “我有了吗？” needs context to convey pregnancy; on its own, it is ambiguous.

column2: I have a certain amount of money on me.
column4: “我有些钱” means “I have some money”; it doesn’t say the money is on me.

column2: I have a good idea.
column4: “我有好主意” is unnatural here; “我有个好主意” is the usual phrasing.

column2: I have a lot of arcade machines.
column4: 电玩通常指电子游戏，不是街机或街机游戏机（arcade machines）。

column2: I'm greening out.
column4: “醉烟” is not a natural expression here; a speaker would more likely say “有点晕烟”.

column2: I must talk to you.
column4: The Chinese says “I have something to tell you,” not necessarily “I must talk to you.”

column1: 我本来应该读一下这本书。
column2: Of course I should read this book.
column4: 本来应该 means “should have,” not “of course should.”

column2: I'm feeding my baby.
column4: “孩子” means a child; “baby” adds the more specific meaning of an infant.

column2: I am pronouncing Chinese words.
column4: The Chinese says the speaker is reading Chinese characters, not pronouncing Chinese words.

column1: 我每天早上在公园写作。
column2: In the morning, I write in the park.
column4: “我每天早上” means “every morning,” but the English does not specify that it happens every day.

column2: I'll call you every night.
column4: 我每晚都给你打电话 means “I call you every night,” not “I'll call you every night.”

column1: 我比较讨厌男人说脏话。
column2: I quite hate it when men use foul language.
column4: “Quite hate” is an unnatural phrasing here; “really dislike” would be more idiomatic.

column2: I couldn't control my anger.
column4: 我气坏了 means “I was furious” or “I got very angry”; it does not say the speaker couldn't control their anger.

column2: I'm out of cash.
column4: 我没带现金 means “I didn’t bring any cash,” not necessarily that I’m out of cash.

column2: I didn't mean to yell.
column4: 我没想叫的 is not a natural way to say “I didn’t mean to yell.”

column2: I didn't mean to capitalize this.
column4: “我没想大写的” is unnatural and incomplete as a standalone sentence.

column2: I didn't mean to break it.
column4: “我没想弄坏的”说法不自然；可说“我不是故意弄坏的”。

column2: I didn't mean to disgust anyone.
column4: “感到不适” means feel uncomfortable, not necessarily feel disgusted.

column2: I'm not upset about her.
column4: 没有对她失望 means “I’m not disappointed in her,” not “I’m not upset about her.”

column2: I didn't mean to be selfish.
column4: “我没有想要自私” is ungrammatical in this meaning; say “我不是故意自私的” or “我没想自私.”

column1: 我没有见过那男人的印象。
column2: I have no recollection of seeing the man.
column4: “没有见过那男人的印象” is ungrammatical; say “我不记得见过那男人” or “我对见过那男人没有印象.”

column2: I didn't confront them.
column4: 没发生冲突 means they didn't have a conflict, not necessarily that I didn't confront them.

column2: I can swim well.
column4: 语序不自然；通常说“我游泳游得很好”或“我很会游泳”。

column2: I love his smile.
column4: “爱上” means to fall in love with someone or something; it does not simply mean “love” here.

column2: Son, I love you.
column4: “大儿子” specifies the eldest son, which is omitted in the English.

column2: My father made me wash the car.
column4: 我父亲要我洗车 means “My father wants/told me to wash the car,” not that he made me do it.

column1: 我爸和去年比老了不少。
column2: My father aged a lot since last year.
column4: “Aged … since last year” is not natural here; say “has aged a lot since last year.”

column1: 我爸爸不喝太多的烧酒。
column2: My father doesn't drink too much sake.
column4: “烧酒” means distilled liquor, not sake.

column1: 我爸爸昨天带了我去看电影。
column2: My father took me to a movie last night.
column4: “昨天” means “yesterday,” not specifically “last night.”

column1: 我爸爸送了一块电子表给我作为生日礼物。
column2: My father bought me a digital watch for birthday present.
column4: “for birthday present” is ungrammatical; say “as a birthday present.”

column2: My teeth hurt.
column4: “我牙疼” refers to a toothache, while “My teeth hurt” says multiple teeth hurt.

column2: I don't want to talk to you now.
column4: The word order is unnatural; say “我现在不想跟你说话。”

column1: 我用三块钱买了那本书。
column2: I paid 3 dollars for the book.
column4: “三块钱” means three yuan, not three dollars.

column2: I listen to the radio with a receiver.
column4: “With a receiver” is unnatural here; a radio is the natural English term.

column2: I'll pay in cash.
column4: “我用现金付钱” describes paying in cash, while “I'll pay” explicitly places it in the future.

column1: 我申请了国外的研究生。
column2: I applied for grad school abroad.
column4: “申请了国外的研究生” is not a natural way to say applying to graduate school abroad; use “申请了国外的研究生院” or “申请了国外的研究生项目.”

column2: the pictures that I draw / drew
column4: This is a noun phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: I have not more than ten books.
column4: “I have not more than ten books” is awkward; “I have no more than ten books” is natural.

column1: 我的做法是要行动不要空话。
column2: My way is action not words.
column4: “我的做法是要行动不要空话” is unnatural; “我的原则是要行动，不要空话” is more idiomatic.

column2: My taste has gotten heavier.
