column4: The Chinese says there are many things in this that I don’t understand; the English says I don’t understand much about it.

column2: The scenery here is graceful.
column4: 优美 means beautiful or picturesque here, not “graceful.”

column2: This knowledge is solid.
column4: “这门学问很扎实” is an unnatural collocation; “学问扎实” can describe a person's knowledge.

column2: How old is this zoo?
column4: 这间动物园多久了 is unnatural; use 这个动物园有多久了 or 这个动物园有多少年历史了.

column1: 这间学校女孩比男孩多。
column2: There are more girls than boys in this school.
column4: 间 is not the natural classifier for 学校; 所 is standard here.

column2: This store is closed at nine.
column4: The Chinese says the store closes at nine; “is closed at nine” describes its state at that time.

column2: This house must be done up.
column4: “维修” means repair or maintenance; “done up” usually means renovated or redecorated.

column2: How much is this hat?
column4: “帽”作这里的名词不自然；通常说“这顶帽子多少钱？”

column2: This bill is safe to pass.
column4: “安全的通过” is not grammatical here; the adverb would be “安全地,” and the sentence remains unnatural.

column2: I wrote the song for her.
column4: The Chinese is passive and does not say who wrote the song; the English adds “I.”

column2: The fish tasted like salmon.
column4: “这鱼吃著像” is unnatural; say “这鱼吃起来像三文鱼”.

column2: In Progress.
column4: “进行中” is a status phrase, not a complete sentence.

column2: Escape from reality.
column4: This is a sentence fragment rather than a complete sentence.

column2: placeholder
column4: “placeholder” is not a translation of the Chinese sentence.

column2: Toki Pona is reductive.
column4: “属于极简主义” means “belongs to minimalism” or “is minimalist,” not “is reductive.”

column2: Who is this person?
column4: “那一位” means “that person,” not “this person.”

column2: That wasn't very good.
column4: “那不太好” means “That’s not very good,” not specifically “That wasn’t very good.”

column2: It doesn't really matter.
column4: “那不真的重要”不自然；可说“那并不重要”或“那不太重要”。

column2: That wasn't so hard, was it?
column4: 中文通常表示“那不难”，而英文明确说“那当时不难”。

column1: 那个团体为难民们提供食品供给。
column2: The organization furnished the refugees with food.
column4: “提供食品供给” is awkward and redundant. “为难民们提供食品” is natural.

column1: 那个地方我去过数十次了。
column2: I went there dozens of times.
column4: “去过” expresses having been there (an experience); “I went there” describes a past trip.

column1: 那个小偷在公交车上摸到了一部手机。
column2: That thief stole a phone on the bus.
column4: 摸到 means touched or felt; it does not mean stole.

column2: That trip is expensive.
column4: “那个旅行” is unnatural; say “那趟旅行” or “那次旅行”.

column2: That box is made of wood.
column4: “用木造的” is unnatural here; say “用木头做的” or “木制的.”

column1: 那个药的话没有处方是买不到的。
column2: You can't buy this medicine without a prescription.
column4: “那个药” means “that medicine,” not “this medicine.”

column1: 那么,让我们开始进行吧。
column2: Well, let's get the ball rolling.
column4: 开始进行 is awkward and redundant here; a natural phrasing is 那么，让我们开始吧。

column1: 那么你下午到过几个地方？
column2: So how many places have you been to in the afternoon?
column4: “Have you been to … in the afternoon” is awkward; “How many places did you visit this afternoon?” is natural.

column1: 那么你频道换掉也行啊。
column2: You can just switch channels.
column4: The word order is unnatural. Say “你把频道换掉也行啊” or “你换个频道也行啊。”

column2: Those men are speaking French.
column4: “那些人” means “those people,” not specifically “those men.”

column1: 那些钱藏了在地板下面。
column2: The money was hidden beneath the floorboards.
column4: “藏了在” is ungrammatical here; say “藏在地板下面”.

column1: 那件衣服是你两个月的工资，买得起吗？
column2: That piece of clothing is worth two months of your salary. Can you afford to buy it?
column4: The Chinese says the clothing costs two months’ salary, while “is worth” describes its value.

column2: that new computer
column4: 那台电脑 means “that computer”; the English adds that it is new.

column2: Where did you go that night?
column4: 那天晚上你在哪里？ asks where you were, not where you went.

column2: The shop is just in front of the station.
column4: 正对着 means directly facing or opposite the station, not simply in front of it.

column2: Is your sister older than you?
column4: The Chinese asks whether she is the older or younger sister; the English asks only whether she is older.

column1: 那是我一生中最美好的时光之一。
column2: That is one of my best time in my life.
column4: “One of my best time” should be “one of my best times.”

column2: The tree was ready to fall at any moment.
column4: 随时会倒下来 describes a possible imminent fall, not a past state of being ready to fall.

column2: That feels good.
column4: 那看来很好 means “That seems/looks good,” not “That feels good.”

column1: 那真是很热、很热的夜晚。
column2: It was a very, very hot night.
column4: “很热、很热” is not a natural way to repeat the adjective here; say “很热很热” or “非常非常热”.

column2: What's the idea behind that?
column4: “那背后是什么意思” is awkward; “那背后的意思是什么” is more natural.

column2: That street is very noisy.
column4: “那街道” is unnatural here; say “那条街道”.

column2: Does that make me weird?
column4: “那让我奇怪吗”不自然；可说“那会让我显得很奇怪吗？”

column2: City life is fast.
column4: “都市的生活很快” is not a natural way to say that city life is fast-paced.

column2: It's because of you, making me go all that way.
column4: “It's because of you, making me go all that way” is awkwardly constructed; “It's all your fault for making me go all that way” is natural.

column2: Take his way.
column4: “Take his way” is not a natural English expression for adopting someone’s method.

column2: Money answers all things.
column4: “钱是万能的” means money can do anything; “answers all things” does not convey that meaning.

column1: 钱是他想要的最后的东西。
column2: Money is the last thing he wants.
column4: This is an unnatural way to express “Money is the last thing he wants.”

column2: A new lamp was installed over the door.
column4: “安了一个新灯” is unnatural; “装了一盏新灯” would be more natural.

column2: Prevention is better than cure.
column4: “防胜于治” is not a natural expression; “预防胜于治疗” is standard.

column1: 阳光照亮田野，痛苦点亮心灵。
column2: Sun lights the landscape, pain illuminates the soul.
column4: “Sun” needs an article here: “The sun lights the landscape.”

column1: 阿尔及利亚仍国境贫困。
column2: Algeria is still poor.
column4: 阿尔及利亚仍国境贫困 is ungrammatical and does not naturally express “Algeria is still poor.”

column1: 阿尔及利亚是四千万人口大国。
column2: Algeria is a big country of forty million inhabitants.
column4: “四千万人口大国” is not a natural construction; say “有四千万人口的大国.”

column1: 除了苏打水，我什么都不喝。
column2: I never drank anything but soda.
column4: The Chinese describes a habitual preference, while the English says “never drank,” in the past.

column2: Suit yourself.
column4: 随你开心 is unnatural in this context; a natural phrase is 随你高兴.

column1: 难怪他，他还是个孩子呢，什么都不懂。
column2: Don't blame him, he's just a child. He doesn't know any better.
column4: “难怪他” means “no wonder he…,” not “don’t blame him”; the Chinese sentence is not naturally phrased for the intended meaning.

column2: Young people are apt to go to extremes.
column4: “挑战极端” is not a natural expression here; “挑战极限” would mean “challenge limits.”

column1: 靠近一点听，你就会听到了。
column2: If you listen closely enough you'll be able to hear it.
column4: 靠近一点 means to move closer; the English instead says to listen closely enough.

column1: 鞋子是一对一对的卖的。
column2: Shoes are sold in pairs.
column4: “一对一对的卖的” is awkward; use “一双一双地卖” or “一双一双卖的”.

column1: 顾客至上是本公司的经营理念。
column4: The English translation is missing.

column2: Expected to arrive tomorrow.
column4: This is a context-dependent fragment: it does not say who or what is expected to arrive.

column2: The wind is blowing hard.
column4: “风吹得很大” is an unnatural collocation; a native speaker would usually say “风刮得很大” or “风很大.”

column2: Poor appetite; he eats little.
column4: “Poor appetite” is a fragment, and the English adds an unspecified “he.”

column1: 首先介绍自己，其次说说计划。
column2: First introduce yourself, then the plan.
column4: “Then the plan” is an awkward fragment; “then talk about the plan” would be natural.

column2: The prime minister dissolved the Diet.
column4: “国会” means parliament; “the Diet” specifically refers to Japan’s parliament.

column2: Hong Kong is referred to as the Pearl of Asia.
column4: “东方之珠” is conventionally translated as “the Pearl of the Orient,” not “the Pearl of Asia.”

column2: How much is the kilo of bananas?
column4: “How much is the kilo of bananas?” is unnatural; say “How much is a kilo of bananas?”

column2: High tech changed life.
column4: The Chinese states a general fact, while “changed” makes it a past event.

column2: The college entrance exam matters.
column4: The Chinese says the college entrance exam score is important, not that the exam itself matters.

column2: How do ducks call?
column4: “How do ducks call?” is unnatural here; say “What sound do ducks make?”

column2: Could I get some water, please?
column4: The Chinese asks someone to pour a glass of water; the English only asks to get some water.

column1: 麻烦的开头是他草率的评论。
column2: The beginning of the trouble was his careless remark.
column4: “麻烦的开头” is unnatural here; “麻烦的起因” is more idiomatic.

column2: Trouble began immediately.
column4: “说来就来” suggests trouble can arrive at any moment, not that it began immediately.

column1: 黑的电话比白的花钱多。
column2: The black telephone costs more than the white.
column4: “电话花钱多” is unnatural for saying that a phone costs more.

column1: 龙是中国文化中的形象。
column2: The dragon is an image in Chinese culture.
column4: “龙是中国文化中的形象” is awkward; “龙是中国文化中的一种形象” or “龙是中国文化的象征” is more natural.
